Leyline: KV Cache Directives for Agentic Inference

Bole Ma Affiliation: Erlangen National High Performance Computing Center    Jan Eitzinger Affiliation: Erlangen, Germany    Harald Köstler Affiliation: {bole.ma, jan.eitzinger, harald.koestler}@fau.de
Abstract

Modern KV cache management assumes the chatbot workload: prompts arrive once and the cache grows append-only, so prefix caching and forward-only eviction are correct by construction. Agentic LLMs (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024) break this assumption. Their conversations evolve through policy-driven editing: failed tool calls are retried, stale outputs dropped, trajectories pivoted. Two distinct cache problems result. First, identical content moves to new positions between turns, invalidating exact-prefix caches even though the underlying KV would still be valid; recent work on position-independent caching for MLA addresses this reuse problem (Ma et al., 2026). Second, and this paper’s focus, a policy may need to direct the serving system to actively remove or replace a span of cached content and continue without re-prefilling everything that came after. No existing primitive offers this. Production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit (Anthropic, 2025), paying full prefix-recomputation cost; kernel-level eviction methods (Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2024) make their own decisions and cannot accept directives from a policy outside the kernel.

We introduce Leyline, a serving-side primitive that closes this gap. The key insight is that a declarative (span,replacement)(\mathrm{span},\,\mathrm{replacement}) 4-tuple can separate what to edit from how to preserve position correctness. The policy declares the edit and its mode (in-place splice or prefix-trimmed re-prefill for semantic forgetting); an architecture-agnostic interface routes to a per-architecture kernel that restores attention math via a closed-form RoPE-rotation correction. We validate on two legs. On the mechanism side, the splice kernel lifts replay cache-hit by +11.2+11.2 pp and cuts latency by up to 241241 ms by reusing prefix work the prompt edit would otherwise have destroyed. On the policy side, a ten-line truncation rule routed through the same interface lifts agentic solve rate by +14.3+14.3 pp on debug-gym, because shorter contexts let the model attend to the few turns that actually matter. The mechanism is open; the policy space it enables is the agenda.

1 Introduction

Agentic LLMs create two distinct cache problems: reuse across natural position shifts, and policy-driven mutation. Prior work addresses the first; this paper addresses the second.

KV cache management research has been organized around one workload assumption: prompts arrive once and the cache grows monotonically. The major optimizations in this lineage (prefix caching (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024), streaming attention (Xiao et al., 2024), attention-based eviction (Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023; Ge et al., 2024)) are correct because the conversation only moves forward: once a token has been prefilled, neither its content nor its position will ever change. The agentic era (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024) breaks this monotonicity assumption in two distinct ways, each producing a different cache-management problem.

Problem 1: position-invariant reuse.

A multi-turn coding or web-research agent re-renders its conversation history every turn. As new tool outputs and retrieved documents land, previously-seen content shifts to new absolute positions. Exact-prefix matching cannot recover these shifted-but-identical chunks, even though their KV would be reusable if the cache were addressed by content rather than position. Recent MLA-native work (Ma et al., 2026) attempted to solve this reuse problem.

Problem 2: policy-driven mutation.

Distinct from reuse, an agent or policy may need to direct the serving system to actively remove or replace cached content: clear a failed tool call’s output, summarize a stale investigation block to a stub, truncate aged tool outputs to free working memory. These are deliberate edits, not natural shifts. Today, agentic harnesses handle them by editing the message list and re-prefilling, because no primitive exists for policy-issued cache editing. The cost is the full prefix-recomputation that prefix caching was meant to amortize, and even small per-request invariant breaks can collapse throughput in production (Cole, 2026).

Our solution.

We introduce Leyline, a serving-side primitive for policy-driven cache editing. The interface is a declarative (span,replacement)(\mathrm{span},\,\mathrm{replacement}) directive in which the policy describes what to edit, while the kernel applies the edit in place via a closed-form δ\delta-rotation. The intuition is one line: when a splice changes downstream absolute positions by Δ\Delta, every cached KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} value at those positions can be rotated by Δ\Delta to restore attention-math correctness, without re-prefilling anything that did not actually change.

What is borrowed, what is new. The numerical kernel (δ\delta-rotation under RoPE closure R⁡(a)​R​(b)=R⁡(a+b)R(a)R(b){=}R(a{+}b) on the MLA KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} band) is from Ma et al. (2026), where it was triggered reactively by a content-hash match on naturally shifted but content-identical chunks (the reuse problem). Leyline’s contribution is the layer that surrounds the kernel: (a) the framing that identifies mutation as a distinct sub-problem from reuse, (b) the declarative directive abstraction that lets a policy invoke the same correction actively as an explicit edit, (c) a 4-tuple contract with declared semantic mode that lets a policy choose between in-place amortization and forgetting-mode re-prefill at the API level (Section 3.1), and (d) the radix-cache integration that preserves the unchanged prefix subtree across the edit. The kernel is the recycled engineering substrate; the directive layer is the new interface boundary the paper argues post-agentic serving stacks need.

Contributions.

(1) A precise distinction between the reuse and mutation problems in agentic KV cache management, locating prior work and identifying mutation as the open sub-problem.

(2) The directive abstraction: a 4-tuple (span,replacement)(\mathrm{span},\,\mathrm{replacement}) interface with declared semantic mode and a pluggable policy layer that decouples what to edit (policy) from how to splice it (kernel), composed over the borrowed δ\delta-rotation correctness mechanism without recomputing the unchanged prefix.

(3) A semantic-edit channel as a new serving-stack interface: the directive sits above block-level KV storage as a span-level edit layer, decomposing each agent-emitted edit into block-level operations the storage layer schedules, and identifies the cache-edit channel as the missing post-agentic interface boundary (Section 7).

(4) Two-leg validation. The directive abstraction earns its keep only if it both runs at production scale and produces a policy-layer signal a deployer would care about. We test each leg separately, then read them together.

(i) Mechanism. A three-arm message-edit microbenchmark on the live SGLang scheduler (cache-off / standard radix / Leyline splice) at ≈17\approx 17 K-token prompts shows the splice arm lifting replay cache-hit rate by +11.2+11.2 pp over the standard radix baseline, uniformly across concurrencies C∈{1,4,8,16}C\in\{1,4,8,16\} and reproducing on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and JoyAI-LLM Flash. The end-to-end latency win peaks at −241-241 ms at C=8C{=}8, where prefill contention is high enough that the saved re-prefill is on the critical path (Appendix B). The point is not the raw number; it is that an explicit edit no longer has to throw away the prefix that the edit did not touch.

(ii) Policy. A ten-line truncation policy routed through the directive interface lifts agentic solve rate by +14.3+14.3 pp over a no-truncation baseline across 88 debug-gym (Yuan et al., 2025) mini_nightmare tasks ×\times 4 seeds ×\times 2 policies on JoyAI-LLM Flash (Section 5). The gain comes from a familiar effect: when stale tool turns are dropped, the model attends to the few turns that actually matter. The interface is what makes the gain cheap to obtain; without it, exercising the same policy would force a full re-prefill on every truncation.

Read together: the mechanism enables the policy class without prefill recompute cost, and the policy class delivers the deployment-cell win. Kernel correctness is separately established on a constructed single-prompt microbenchmark and a cross-architecture MLA replay across four models, with Moonlight as the row where the two references diverge non-trivially (Section 4). Extending the kernel to GQA appears feasible via a boundary-recomputation pass (Hu et al., 2025) and is sketched in Section 6.

2 Background: where existing systems fit

Table 1 positions representative systems against the two sub-problems plus three properties any agentic-era cache primitive needs: correctness after edit, cache-reuse after edit, and turn-granular operation.

The first row trades cache reuse to get correctness on mutation. The second row addresses neither sub-problem. The third (LMCache) is the production storage and movement layer for vLLM and SGLang (Liu et al., 2025) but operates below the semantic-edit level. The fourth and fifth (CacheBlend, EPIC) are the MHA-side analogs to Irminsul’s MLA-side δ\delta-rotation: both address non-prefix reuse on MHA/GQA via selective recomputation rather than positional correction. CacheBlend dynamically picks high-deviation tokens layer-by-layer (Yao et al., 2024); EPIC statically picks each chunk’s first kk tokens, motivated by the attention-sink effect at chunk boundaries (Hu et al., 2025). The sixth trades correctness for speed. The seventh (Irminsul) handles the MLA reuse half; the eighth (Leyline) contributes the mutation half, with CacheBlend/EPIC-style boundary recomputation as the natural mechanism-layer extension we envision for GQA (Section 6).

Layered relationship to LMCache.

LMCache and Leyline operate at different layers and compose. LMCache’s verbs (Pin, Clear, Move, Compress, Lookup) act on KV blocks in physical storage tiers (Liu et al., 2025); Leyline’s directive acts on semantic spans of the prompt. The two meet in the middle of one pipeline: a directive “replace this stale tool-output span with a stub” decomposes into block-level operations (free, allocate, KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} rotate, re-index) that LMCache schedules across tiers. Read end-to-end, this is agent intent →\to semantic directive (L​e​y​l​i​n​eLeyline) →\to block operations (LMCache) →\to physical tier movement. Leyline supplies what LMCache does not: position-encoding correctness across a semantic edit, and a span-level interface for the policy to address. Adjacent work on tensor-encoded KV transfer (Liu et al., 2024a) and 2-bit KV quantization (Liu et al., 2024b) is orthogonal to position correctness.

2.1 Concurrent work on agentic context management

Two recent systems offer signal-side contributions complementary to Leyline’s mechanism: SideQuest (Kariyappa and Suh, 2026) fine-tunes a detector that emits del_cursors commands evicting stale tool-call/response pairs; LoopGuard (Xu et al., 2026) detects decoder-side degeneration symptoms (action repetition, top-1 streak, gzip compressibility) and intervenes by resampling. Either signal can drive Leyline directives without retraining the kernel or the detector. A full taxonomy of useful agentic-era eviction signals is follow-up work.

Framework-engineering signals.

Four open vLLM RFCs each request a slice of cache control at the layer above the storage backend, with no maintainer-accepted abstraction; Leyline’s directive is the missing layer (full thread analysis: App. L).

3 Leyline: a directive abstraction for policy-driven cache editing

Leyline is a serving-side abstraction layer between the agent’s policy and the KV cache. The contributions of this section are three: a declarative directive interface (Section 3.1) that decouples policy signal from kernel mechanism, a serving-stack integration that preserves the radix prefix across edits (Section 3.3), and a thin Python policy interface that any span-emitting policy can drive (Section 3.4). The kernel-level correctness mechanism, the δ\delta-rotation rule that re-anchors cached KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} values after a position shift, is recapped in Section 3.2. Leyline is what turns that rule into a usable primitive for explicit policy-driven editing.

Three properties from Section 2 fix the success criteria, and no existing system meets all three at once. First, signal-agnosticism: the primitive must accept anything expressible as a set of spans, without privileging where the signal came from (Kariyappa and Suh, 2026; Xu et al., 2026), so today’s detector does not constrain tomorrow’s. Second, positional replay-equivalent correctness: after the edit, downstream attention math must be well-formed at the new positions (Section 3.1 makes the contract precise). Third, cache-friendliness: the edit must localize to the spliced span without invalidating the radix prefix, so that the work the prompt edit did not touch survives the edit.

3.1 The directive: (span,replacement)(\mathrm{span},\,\mathrm{replacement})

A directive is a 4-tuple D=(sstart,send,R,m)D=(s_{\mathrm{start}},\,s_{\mathrm{end}},\,R,\,m), where [sstart,send)[s_{\mathrm{start}},s_{\mathrm{end}}) is the token-index range in the original rendered prompt being replaced, RR is the replacement token sequence (often a short stub, e.g. [evicted: 3 older tool turns]), and m∈{amortize,forget}m\in\{\textsc{amortize},\,\textsc{forget}\} selects the semantic mode (we write (span,replacement)(\mathrm{span},\,\mathrm{replacement}) in running text when mm is the default amortize). Multiple non-overlapping directives may be applied per turn. The amortize-mode contract is positional, not informational: after applying DD, the cache produces outputs equivalent to one built from the original prompt with downstream positions reindexed by Δ=|R|−(send−sstart)\Delta=|R|-(s_{\mathrm{end}}-s_{\mathrm{start}}). Concretely, KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} is rotated to the new positions, while KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}} and VV are preserved (they were computed under attention to the original chunk during prefill, and that attention is exactly what we want to keep). Downstream behavior thus reflects the cache’s persistent attention to the original chunk, not the stub. This is deliberately weaker than “equivalent to re-prefill of the substituted prompt”, because re-prefill is precisely the cost the directive amortizes. Section 4 reports empirical agreement against both the full-context baseline (the contract) and the re-prefill path (the stricter contract amortize does not promise), so the reader can see what each path actually predicts.

The forget mode.

Some policies need true content forgetting: redaction of sensitive content, retention-mandated deletion, or correction of an upstream tool error whose continued influence would mislead the agent. These declare m=forgetm=\textsc{forget}, and the serving stack routes the edit to a standard prefix-trimmed re-prefill, the regime production stacks already implement. The directive layer’s addition is the declared intent: the policy says which guarantee it needs, much as a database client declares isolation level rather than relying on serving-side defaults. The empirical validation in this paper is for the amortize path, which carries the engineering novelty; forget adds no new kernel work and is included in the contract specifically to head off the “hidden cache influence” failure mode the abstraction would otherwise enable. Governance patterns built on the mode distinction are detailed in App. O.

Which tensors are modified.

The kernel frees KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}}/KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}}/VV at the evicted span, freshly prefills K and VV for the replacement RR, and rotates only KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} of downstream slots by Δ\Delta (Equation 1); KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}} and VV of those slots are untouched. Decode-time Q is recomputed each step, so no Q reindexing is needed. Attention-sink prefixes are unaffected provided sstarts_{\mathrm{start}} sits past them. The full step-by-step specification and the confounder-rule-out argument are in Appendix C.

The directive interface is signal-agnostic. Anything producing (sstart,send,R)(s_{\mathrm{start}},s_{\mathrm{end}},R) tuples drives the cache; the kernel does not inspect the rationale. This is property (i)’s policy/mechanism decoupling in concrete form, distinct from Irminsul’s content-hash-triggered reuse: a policy that says “drop this aged tool output” is an explicit edit, not a hash hit, and needs an agent-facing invocation path portable across serving stacks. One policy family is instantiated in Section 5.

3.2 The δ\delta-rotation foundation (recap)

The reason the kernel can correct a splice so cheaply is structural. Under MLA, cached K splits into KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}} (no position) and KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} (rotated by RoPE by absolute position) (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2024a; Su et al., 2024): Kpe​[i]=R⁡(i)⋅Kperaw​[i]K_{\mathrm{pe}}[i]=R(i)\cdot K_{\mathrm{pe}}^{\mathrm{raw}}[i]. Position lives in a single rotated slice; everything else in the cache is position-free already. After a directive splices a replacement of length |R||R| in place of [sstart,send)[s_{\mathrm{start}},s_{\mathrm{end}}), every downstream token at position i≥sendi\geq s_{\mathrm{end}} shifts by Δ=|R|−(send−sstart)\Delta=|R|-(s_{\mathrm{end}}-s_{\mathrm{start}}). The δ\delta-rotation rule of Ma et al. (2026) corrects this in closed form:

Kpenew​[i]=R⁡(Δ)⋅Kpe​[i],K_{\mathrm{pe}}^{\mathrm{new}}[i]=R(\Delta)\cdot K_{\mathrm{pe}}[i], (1)

which equals the KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} that an honest prefill at position i+Δi+\Delta would have produced, by RoPE’s unitary-rotation closure R⁡(a)​R​(b)=R⁡(a+b)R(a)R(b)=R(a+b). The closure is what does the work: applying R⁡(Δ)R(\Delta) on top of R⁡(i)R(i) is algebraically indistinguishable from having computed R⁡(i+Δ)R(i+\Delta) in the first place. The correction is one matmul per slot, and KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}} is untouched. The single-rotation bf16 drift bound (4.7×10−34.7{\times}10^{-3} rel-L2) is from Ma et al. (2026); chained rotations accumulate sub-linearly under composition (Numerics., App. F).

3.3 Serving-stack integration

Each directive triggers three steps inside the serving stack (Figure 2), each handling a distinct region of the prompt. (1) For tokens before sstarts_{\mathrm{start}}, the radix cache matches the prompt as usual; the unedited prefix survives the edit, and this is the source of Leyline’s cache-reuse property. (2) For the replacement itself, tokens RR are prefilled fresh into newly allocated slots at positions [sstart,sstart+|R|)[s_{\mathrm{start}},s_{\mathrm{start}}+|R|). (3) For tokens after the edit, cached KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} for slots originally at i≥sendi\geq s_{\mathrm{end}} is rotated by Δ\Delta (Equation 1) and reindexed to i+Δi+\Delta. Only the third step touches cached state, and it does so with a single matmul per slot.

The mechanism is implemented in two paths that share one rotation kernel. The rotation kernel itself is a single in-place operation on the KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} band of a transformers DynamicCache; we verify against DSv2-Lite’s native rotary_emb that the kernel is bit-exact for a single rotation, and this same kernel is the source of truth for all empirical claims below.

RoPE pairing convention.

RoPE admits two pairing conventions in active use: interleaved (GPT-J style, mixing dims 2​i2i and 2​i+12i{+}1) and half-split (NEOX style, mixing dims ii and i+d/2i{+}d/2). DSv2-Lite’s MLA uses interleaved; Llama- and Qwen2-style models use half-split. The kernel reads rotary_is_neox_style per layer and applies the matching pairing; mismatched pairing leaves Kpe⋅cosK_{\mathrm{pe}}\,{\cdot}\,\cos correct but corrupts the sin\sin-rotated half, hiding at Δ≈0\Delta{\approx}0 (where sin⁡(Δ​f)→0\sin(\Delta f){\to}0) and growing with |Δ||\Delta|. We validated the post-fix kernel bit-exact against full prefill across Δ∈{1,21,48,76,512,2000}\Delta\in\{1,21,48,76,512,2000\}, and end-to-end across |Δ||\Delta| up to ≈4531\approx 4531 (target positions past original_max_position_embeddings=4096{=}4096 into the YaRN-interpolated regime), on DSv2-Lite. For NEOX-style models the new convention-aware path is arithmetically identical to the prior code.

Role B: edits via radix-trie insertion.

Two integration paths share the rotation kernel of the previous paragraph. Role A returns a patched MatchResult from a wrapped match_prefix, injecting borrowed slots that the request frees at completion. Role B (implemented in the SGLang patch) goes one layer further: after a successful splice, the patch calls tree_cache.insert(InsertParams(key=token_ids[:cur_end], value=concat(orig_indices, dst_slots))) and re-runs the un-wrapped match_prefix so the returned match is a native, longer trie hit. Slot lifetime then moves to the radix trie’s lock_ref and eviction policy, retiring the borrowed-slot orphan-detection. The mechanism is gated by AKASHA_PIC_ROLE_B_L2=1; it is correctness-clean on our validation and is the path that makes spliced KV discoverable to future requests via vanilla match_prefix, without a PIC hook at lookup time. The complete spec is in App. R.

(i) The offline replay kernel (used in Section 4) loads the model via HuggingFace transformers and applies the rotation in process; it is the path against which we report replay-equivalence and randomized-edit stress. (ii) A ∼200{\sim}200-LOC SGLang RadixCache patch populates a content-hash side index inside the live engine and routes matched directives through the same rotation kernel at the KV-pool allocator level; this is the path exercised by the three-arm microbenchmark of App. B. The directive abstraction itself is architecture-agnostic; only the rotation kernel is MLA-specific (Section 6).

Multiple directives.

A turn may carry several non-overlapping directives; the kernel processes them left-to-right and the rotation algebra closes under composition (R⁡(Δ1)​R​(Δ2)=R⁡(Δ1+Δ2)R(\Delta_{1})R(\Delta_{2}){=}R(\Delta_{1}{+}\Delta_{2})), with Δ\Delta of either sign. Full composition and allocator rules are in App. C.

3.4 The policy interface

The directive abstraction admits any policy that maps conversation state to a directive list. We expose a thin Python abstraction with a single Policy.transform(messages, turn_idx) →\to messages method; Leyline computes the diff against the previous turn and applies it through the kernel mechanism of Section 3.3. A policy can be a turn-counter, a hand rule, a content-pattern matcher, or any function over conversation state.

4 Demonstrating correctness for the mutation operation

Prior work establishes the δ\delta-rotation as correct by construction for position shifts in the reuse case (Ma et al., 2026); the directive-driven splice must produce the same guarantee under arbitrary edit patterns. The load-bearing test is the constructed single-prompt microbenchmark of Section 4.1. Its design is the point: the elided content is chosen so that the full-context and re-prefill references must disagree on the next token, making the contract’s distinguishing prediction (Leyline tracks full-context, not re-prefill) directly observable on the first decoded token. The remaining empirical material adds workload coverage: a 12-step policy-derived trajectory replayed across four MLA architectures, a randomized synthetic edit-suite over arbitrary span positions and signed Δ\Delta, kernel-level chained-rotation drift, and 50-step long-horizon trajectories. These tests live in the appendix; Section 4.2 summarizes the headline numbers.

4.1 Single-prompt replay equivalence

This subsection carries the central correctness claim. The setup is a constructed microbenchmark where the references are guaranteed to disagree, so the contract’s distinguishing prediction (Section 3.1: Leyline tracks full, not re-prefill) is testable by construction. The appendix coverage adds architectural and workload breadth but inherits its interpretive weight from here.

Setup. A prompt asks the model to recall a calculation buried mid-prompt. The chunk is the literal calculation 25+9=3425+9=34 (57 tokens), wrapped by 5 pre-tokens and 9 post-tokens, with the answer requested at the post-decode position. A directive replaces the calculation chunk with the 11-token stub [truncated] (Δ=−46\Delta{=}-46). Three paths are compared: full-context (original prompt prefilled honestly), re-prefill (stub-substituted prompt prefilled honestly), and Leyline (original prompt prefilled, then directive applied via δ\delta-rotation).

Result. The full-context path predicts ’34’ (the correct answer); re-prefill predicts ’0’ (the model lost the calculation when the stub replaced it); Leyline predicts ’34’ (it tracks the full-context cache). This is the positional contract from Section 3.1 in action. Leyline preserves the downstream slots’ KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}} and VV, which were computed under attention to the original chunk, so the cache continues to drive the model toward the chunk-informed output. Re-prefill instead rebuilds those slots’ KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}} and VV against the stub, losing the calculation’s effect on downstream attention. The fact that Leyline tracks full-context, not re-prefill, is therefore the contract, not a bug. A kernel that tracked re-prefill would have to recompute all downstream K/V; that is exactly the prefill cost the directive is designed to avoid.

A 4×3×24{\times}3{\times}2 ablation (stub modes ×\times trajectories ×\times models) confirms the rotation, not stub text, is load-bearing (Appendix M). All decodes here are greedy (argmax, no sampling); model weights are bf16 under stock HuggingFace forward passes; the three paths share identical model and tokenizer state, so observed differences arise only from the cache state at the prefill-to-decode boundary.

bf16 K-storage precision floor.

Independent of rotation precision, the bf16 KV pool itself imposes a structural floor on per-K-entry accuracy. Sweeping the rotation kernel at source positions up to 88368836 and |Δ||\Delta| up to 67946794 on DSv2-Lite, we measure a uniform ∼\sim1–3% per-entry error from bf16 storage, independent of Δ\Delta, vs fp32 where the same kernel returns <10−3<\!10^{-3} error at every tested (p,Δ)(p,\Delta). This floor causes occasional argmax flips: on a 50-step long-context agentic replay (App. B), Leyline matches a full-prefill reference on 48/5048/50 first-token outputs. The mismatches occur on prompts whose top-1/top-2 logit gap is below the bf16 floor; the failure direction is not biased (the same workload’s no-splice path occasionally lands on a different argmax for the same reason). We default AKASHA_PIC_ROTATION_FP32=1 so the rotation computation runs in fp32 (matching the model’s own attention-forward precision policy) even when the KV pool stores bf16; this removes the rotation’s contribution to the floor but does not eliminate the storage’s contribution. The honest claim is bit-faithfulness within bf16 precision: outputs are byte-identical to a full prefill only on prompts with logit-margin above the noise floor. The full per-position error table and the fp32-mitigation decomposition are in App. Q.

4.2 Coverage summary

Four additional tests add architectural and workload breadth.

(i) A 12-step counter-trajectory replay across four MLA models (DSv2-Lite, JoyAI-LLM Flash, GLM-4.7-Flash, Moonlight-16B-A3B), with greedy 128-token decodes at each step. The kernel never changes tool selection (15/1515/15 tool-name agreement on both-parseable edit steps), and on the one step where the two references diverge (Moonlight) Leyline tracks full-context as predicted (App. D, Table 4). Beyond first-token agreement, the mean common-prefix length of the 128-token decode tells a more graded story: 128/128128/128 on DSv2-Lite (paths bit-equivalent), 42/12842/128 on JoyAI, 6/1286/128 on GLM (low because a first-token disagreement diverges the suffix early), and 75/12875/128 on Moonlight against full-context versus 50/12850/128 against re-prefill. That last comparison is the interesting one: on the model where the two references actually separate, Leyline sits closer to full-context than to re-prefill, exactly the ordering the contract predicts.

(ii) A randomized stress suite over signed Δ\Delta and 1–2 edits per turn confirms the prediction on Moonlight: 14/1714/17 random-stub and 11/1311/13 semantic-stub diverging trials track full-context, while 00 track re-prefill. DSv2-Lite is invariant under the suite (the two references rarely diverge in the first place), and JoyAI and GLM exhibit a position-axis sensitivity to mid-template splices that policy-derived edits do not trigger (App. E, Table 5). Positive-Δ\Delta insertions appear at uniform sampling (each replacement length is drawn from [0,2​|span|][0,2|\mathrm{span}|], so Δ>0\Delta{>}0 on roughly half the trials), and the qualitative pattern is the same on both signs: references diverge non-trivially on Moonlight, are invariant on DSv2, and react to mid-template position on JoyAI/GLM.

(iii) Chained rotations on the same logical slot grow sub-linearly in bf16 (6.1×6.1{\times} rel-L2 growth across a 50×50{\times} rotation-count increase up to N=100N{=}100; App. F); a 50-step long-horizon trajectory preserves first-token agreement at 100%100\% on DSv2-Lite, ≥ 80%{\geq}\,80\% on GLM, ∼56%{\sim}56\% on Moonlight, with JoyAI degrading on tokens but preserving tool-name at 6767–72%72\% (App. G, Table 7).

(iv) Per-step logit-level distances are consistent with the argmax picture: where argmax matches, KL is below 0.50.5 nats (App. I). The model-side sensitivities we observe are documented as model behavior, not kernel correctness gaps, and are addressable via the boundary-token recomputation discussed in Section 6.

5 Deployment-cell evidence at the policy layer

The directive interface’s value depends on a measurable policy-layer signal: a ∼\sim10-line truncation policy routed through the interface should improve agentic task behavior over a no-truncation baseline. The mechanism we expect is straightforward. As a debugging trajectory grows, most of the older tool output is stale; dropping it frees the model’s attention to focus on the small slice that still matters. Across 8 debug-gym (Yuan et al., 2025) mini_nightmare tasks ×\times 4 seeds on JoyAI-LLM Flash under the standard re-prefill arm (32 baseline + 33 treatment trials), the truncation treatment lifts solve rate from 10/32=31.2%10/32=31.2\% (baseline) to 15/33=45.5%15/33=45.5\% (treatment), a +14.3+14.3 pp absolute gain (Table 2). The asymmetry in NN reflects one extra counter trial in the treatment arm; the paired analysis below restricts to the symmetric subset. A ninth task, pandas_dataframe, was excluded because it requires fetching an external dataset over the network and our compute nodes have no outbound internet access; both policies failed equally on every pandas_dataframe trial we ran, so the exclusion is environmental rather than policy-related. Across the 31 paired (task, seed) cells where both arms ran with reliable provenance, both policies agree on 17 outcomes; of the 14 cells where they disagree, the treatment wins 9 and the baseline wins 5 (1.8×1.8\times asymmetry). Where the gain concentrates is consistent with the hypothesis: the two tasks with substantial trajectory length, shopping_cart (0%→75%0\%\to 75\%) and sum_tree (25%→50%25\%\to 50\%), do all the work. On tasks that are either too short to trigger truncation or hard enough that neither policy solves them under the 50-step cap, the curves overlap.

These are properties of the truncation policy routed through standard message-edit semantics; they do not isolate any contribution from Leyline’s splice kernel, whose correctness is established independently by Section 4. This is the policy leg of the two-leg validation.

Mechanism leg, at production scale.

App. B reports the mechanism leg under controlled prompts: a three-arm SGLang microbenchmark on DeepSeek-V2-Lite at ∼\sim17 K-token prompts, batch-scaled across C∈{1,4,8,16}C\in\{1,4,8,16\}. The splice arm produces a uniform +11.2+11.2 pp replay cache-hit gain over standard radix at every concurrency, with the e2e p50 latency win peaking at −241-241 ms (−4.4%-4.4\%) at C=8C{=}8, where prefill contention is high relative to the decode tail; at C=1C{=}1 the saved prefill runs in serial with decode (smaller absolute win), and at C=16C{=}16 it is absorbed into the now decode-dominated tail. Cross-arm first-token argmax agreement against radix holds at 100%/97.7%/98.4%/94.5%100\%/97.7\%/98.4\%/94.5\% across the four cells, matching the cache-off-vs-radix reference floor (two paths sharing no directive code), so the splice path tracks the warm-prefix path at the noise floor of batched bf16 scheduling, not at a directive-layer correctness gap. Together, the mechanism enables the policy class at lower prefill recompute cost; the policy class delivers the deployment-cell win. Per-task discussion and the policy-loaded provenance check are in App. A.

Real-trace e2e (long-context agentic replay).

The synthetic microbenchmark above isolates the mechanism leg under fixed prompts. We additionally replay a 50-step debug-gym agentic trajectory (07be28b9/shopping_cart, prompts growing from 334 to ∼28{\sim}28K tokens, C=1C{=}1) through the same three-arm setup. Vanilla SGLang RadixCache reaches sum-e2e 52.6552.65 s with 27.6%27.6\% cache-hit; Leyline (Role B Level 2 + fp32 rotation) reaches 49.8549.85 s with 27.8%27.8\% cache-hit and 48/5048/50 first-token argmax agreement against the radix arm. The 5.3%5.3\% e2e improvement is the splice’s contribution on top of the prefix-extension hits RadixCache already absorbs. Decomposing the new code shows ∼\sim95% of the timing win is attributable to the fp32 rotation mitigation (Section 4, App. Q); Role B Level 2 is timing-neutral on the single-trajectory scale, since L2’s compound benefit appears only once future-request match coverage compounds across many requests. On a second trajectory (0f724375/shopping_cart, 91.6%91.6\% RadixCache hit-rate) the splice is 0.6%0.6\% slower than radix and 20/2020/20 bit-identical; when RadixCache already covers the workload, there is no headroom for the splice to use. The takeaway is that the wins are workload-conditional. Substantial divergent tails are the regime where splice helps, because they are exactly the cases where vanilla prefix matching is doing the least; RadixCache-friendly traces, by definition, leave nothing on the table.

Cross-tenant at production concurrency.

At C=4C{=}4 on a cross-tenant Zipf workload (two tenants, 8 articles, 15001500-character bodies, 3232 requests/tenant), the splice’s discovery rate is bottlenecked by a within-batch race: peer requests in the same batch all run match_prefix before any of them has finished, so the popular registry entries are not yet visible to the rest of the batch. Without warm-start, cand_total=6{=}6 and chunks_spliced=2{=}2 across 122122 splice calls. We address this with a manifest warm-start: a JSONL of {content_hash, chunk_tokens, count} serialized from the prior run’s registry, replayed at startup as /generate requests against the live server before the benchmark begins. The same workload then reaches cand_total=96{=}96 and chunks_spliced=16{=}16 (16×16\times and 8×8\times improvements respectively), with tenant-1 e2e p50p_{50} dropping from 1.0161.016 s to 0.9530.953 s (−6.2%-6.2\%). The manifest is small (1515 unique chunks, ∼\sim4 KB) and the warm-up phase completes in ∼1.2{\sim}1.2 s. The implementation is gated by AKASHA_PIC_MANIFEST_OUT (producer) and AKASHA_PIC_MANIFEST_IN (consumer); see App. S. Scope of the warm-start result: we have demonstrated discovery activation in this 2-tenant C=4C{=}4 configuration. Extending to higher tenant counts or higher concurrencies hits an unresolved candidate-filter degenerate: the same warmup-then-workload pattern at 4-tenant C=4C{=}4, 3-tenant C=4C{=}4 (with or without warmup), 8-tenant C=4C{=}4, and 2-tenant C=8C{=}8 all reach cand_total=0{=}0 even when the registry shows 1515–3535 unique observed hashes (jobs 473946473946–473952473952, App. U). The proximate cause is a candidate filter (src_kv_indices is not None and request_id ≠\neq rid_now) that empties when the warmup-time inserts share the population window with the live workload’s observe path. Working past this is concrete follow-up engineering, not a contract issue with the directive abstraction.

KV bytes attributable to splice.

Per-token KV in the DSv2-Lite MLA pool is (kv​_​lora​_​rank+qk​_​rope​_​head​_​dim)×nlayers×2(\mathrm{kv\_lora\_rank}+\mathrm{qk\_rope\_head\_dim})\times n_{\mathrm{layers}}\times 2 bytes =(512+64)×27×2=31,104{=}(512+64)\times 27\times 2=31{,}104 bytes (≈30{\approx}30 KB). On the long-context agentic replay above, the splice arm carries +1,750+1{,}750 tokens of cached content over the radix arm, which corresponds to 52.552.5 MB of KV reused rather than recomputed. On the cross-tenant C=4C{=}4 workload with warm-start, 1616 chunks of 5656 tokens average give 27.927.9 MB of KV reused across 6464 requests, vs 3.983.98 MB without warm-start. The right way to read these figures is as the splice’s incremental contribution to cache content above vanilla RadixCache: they are savings in re-prefill compute and pool writes, not a reduction in peak memory occupancy.

Peak KV pool occupancy and tenant scaling.

We instrumented the SGLang TokenToKVPoolAllocator to sample available_size() on every cache_finished_req/cache_unfinished_req hook (App. U) and swept tenant counts {2,3,4,8}\{2,3,4,8\} at concurrency C=4C{=}4, 88 articles per tenant, on the cross-tenant Zipf workload. The splice-OFF peak occupancies are: 2-tenant 53.653.6 MB, 3-tenant 74.374.3 MB (1.39×1.39\times vs 2-tenant), 4-tenant 97.597.5 MB (1.82×1.82\times), 8-tenant 182.0182.0 MB (3.40×3.40\times). All four numbers fall under the linear projections of 1.5×1.5\times, 2.0×2.0\times, 4.0×4.0\times, because vanilla RadixCache’s prefix-overlap detection is already catching ∼8\sim 8 pp of cross-tenant overlap at 3 tenants and growing to ∼15\sim 15 pp at 8 tenants without any splice contribution. Splice ON does not reduce peak pool occupancy: at 4-tenant the splice-ON and splice-OFF peaks are identical to the slot (3,1353{,}135 slots of 1,698,8461{,}698{,}846); at 8-tenant similarly identical (5,8505{,}850 slots). The reason is structural: Role B inserts spliced chunks into the radix trie by reference rather than freeing pool slots, so the splice’s KV-content advantage shows up as re-prefill compute saved (the 27.927.9 MB cited above), not as concurrent allocator memory dropped. Warm-start, where it activates, adds a small fixed cost: 2-tenant ON + warmup is 65.765.7 MB (+12.0+12.0 MB above splice-OFF, from the warm-up-preloaded articles staying trie-pinned), and 4-tenant ON + warmup is 112.4112.4 MB (+14.9+14.9 MB above splice-OFF) even though the 4-tenant arm itself yields zero spliced chunks (see App. U “Follow-up arm E”). The implications split cleanly by what a workload is bottlenecked on: workloads constrained on allocator pressure should not expect splice to drop their watermark, while workloads constrained on re-prefill compute under high cross-tenant overlap should see the splice’s content advantage only at the discovery-active configuration (C=4C{=}4, 2-tenant, with warm-start), until the candidate-filter generalization above lands.

6 Generalizing beyond MLA: an invitation

We validate on MLA because it admits the cleanest rotation correction: positions are isolated to a 64-dim RoPE-rotated slice KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}}, leaving the bulk of K position-free (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2024a; Ma et al., 2026). The four largest agent-trained open-weight models we evaluated are all MLA (DeepSeek-V2-Lite, JoyAI-LLM Flash, GLM-4.7-Flash, Moonlight-16B-A3B), so the cost of swapping architecture for our purposes was zero. Above the kernel, every layer of Leyline is architecture-agnostic by construction: the directive interface, the radix-cache integration, and the policy interface depend only on token spans, not on how positions are encoded. Only step (3) of Section 3.3, the rotation kernel itself, is MLA-specific.

Extension to GQA and MHA.

RoPE’s unitary-rotation algebra transfers to GQA and MHA (Su et al., 2024); the complication is that they fuse position throughout the full KK tensor rather than isolating it to a slice, so the rotation must act across all dKd_{K} dimensions per token. Algebra-level and live-model validation are in App. H: the kernel runs end-to-end on Llama-3.1-Minitron-4B and Qwen3-4B without numeric issues, but the model-side ill-formed-cache sensitivity we documented on MLA manifests more strongly because rotation acts on dimensions that also carry content. The boundary-recomputation pass of concurrent reuse-side work (Yao et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025) is a candidate kernel-layer addition without changing the directive; non-rotary encodings (ALiBi, NoPE, learned absolute) are future work.

Forward compatibility.

The directive abstraction is mechanism-agnostic; the rotation kernel is not. Within-MLA architecture evolution (e.g. trained sparsity) inherits splice + δ\delta-rotation directly; out-of-MLA evolution (e.g. sequence-compressed KV) breaks the rotation kernel but the span-level directive remains well-typed. Appendix N develops the two concrete DeepSeek cases (V3.2-Exp (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2025), V4 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026)).

7 Discussion

The serving-stack interface boundary moves.

Pre-agentic serving systems had a single interface to the agent layer: the prompt. Post-agentic systems need a second one, a cache-edit channel, which Leyline’s directive defines concretely. The interface decouples policy (“what should be in cache?”) from mechanism (“how to splice the cache to match without re-prefill”), so policies can emit (span,replacement)(\mathrm{span},\,\mathrm{replacement}) without knowing MLA, RoPE, or radix internals.

Composition with concurrent and adjacent work.

Signal-side detectors (SideQuest (Kariyappa and Suh, 2026), LoopGuard (Xu et al., 2026)) and active-RAG retrieval patterns (FLARE (Jiang et al., 2023), Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024), CacheBlend (Yao et al., 2024), EPIC (Hu et al., 2025)) compose naturally with Leyline’s directive interface: any signal expressible as a span-set drives a directive without retraining the kernel or the detector. Furthermore, the recomputation mechanisms of CacheBlend (dynamic high-deviation token selection) and EPIC (static chunk-boundary recomputation) plug in at the kernel layer beneath the directive, providing the GQA/MHA path identified in Section 6. See Appendix K for the detailed mapping.

Safety as an API contract.

Locating the mode declaration (amortize vs forget) at the agent layer rather than the serving stack mirrors how database clients declare isolation level: it moves the choice between in-place amortization and semantic forgetting from hidden serving-stack default to a declared, auditable per-edit contract. Concrete governance patterns and the concurrency/tenant-isolation discussion are in App. O.

Beyond eviction: a programmable memory primitive.

The splice verb validated here is one of several the directive layer naturally hosts (App. J). DECAY declares an aging-out window for tool output the next reasoning step is unlikely to revisit (for example, the read stage’s output once analyze has consumed it), freeing GPU capacity proactively rather than waiting for end-of-request eviction. PIN declares hard retention for context the agent knows it will revisit, converting speculative tool-output prefetch (Nichols et al., 2025) from a probabilistic guess into a declared guarantee; it composes with SHARE to keep a reference codebase reusable across multiple refactoring agents on the same serving stack. SCRATCH carves attention-mask isolation for reasoning that participates in the current step but is reclaimed before the next. A common pattern runs through these verbs: the agent has earlier and more reliable knowledge of context fate than any system-side predictor can infer, and Leyline externalizes that knowledge as a semantic-edit layer above the storage layer. The effect is to turn KV cache management from a reactive eviction problem, where the system guesses, into a cooperative scheduling one, where the agent declares and the storage layer executes.

8 Conclusion

Agentic LLM serving has two cache sub-problems (Section 2): reuse across position shifts (Irminsul (Ma et al., 2026)) and policy-driven mutation (this paper). Leyline addresses mutation through the (span,replacement)(\mathrm{span},\,\mathrm{replacement}) directive, a declarative span-level edit interface composed over a closed-form δ\delta-rotation kernel. The kernel preserves downstream attention against the original chunk while reindexing positions, so the directive can be applied in place without re-prefilling work the edit never touched. The directive abstraction itself is architecture-agnostic, and only the rotation kernel is MLA-clean, with the natural extension to GQA/MHA sketched in Section 6. The longer arc is broader than eviction. Once the agent can declare what should be in cache, the KV cache becomes a programmable memory layer rather than a system-side guess (Section 7). This paper validates one verb in that layer, splice; the vocabulary the directive interface admits is the agenda the abstraction opens.

Limitations

Architecture coverage.

The kernel-side rotation is MLA-specific in its implementation (one matmul on the 64-dim KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} slice). The directive abstraction generalizes, and the rotation algebra transfers to GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023) and MHA at full dKd_{K} width (Section 6, App. H). On live GQA models the rotation acts on dimensions that also carry content, so the same model-side sensitivity to ill-formed cache state observed on MLA manifests more strongly (App. H); a boundary-token recomputation pass (Hu et al., 2025) as a kernel-layer addition is the natural next step, leaving the directive layer unaffected.

Numerics.

The δ\delta-rotation drift bound (4.7×10−34.7{\times}10^{-3} rel-L2 per rotation in bf16) was established in prior work (Ma et al., 2026); RoPE’s unitary-rotation closure R⁡(a)​R​(b)=R⁡(a+b)R(a)R(b)=R(a+b) makes chained applications mathematically equivalent to a single rotation by the sum. Empirically (Appendix F, Table 6) chained bf16 rotations accumulate drift sub-linearly: 100100 chained rotations show 2.6×10−22.6{\times}10^{-2} rel-L2 against a fresh-RoPE-at-target reference, 5.5×5.5{\times} the per-rotation bound for a 100×100{\times} increase in rotation count. Deployments where the same physical slot is re-rotated thousands of times per session would benefit from periodic re-prefill; we have not measured drift in that extreme regime.

Position-arbitrariness sensitivity.

JoyAI and GLM exhibit high model-side sensitivity to position-arbitrary (mid-message, mid-template-tag) splices in the randomized edit-suite (Appendix E); the policy-derived runs splice at chat-message boundaries and the same kernel produces clean tool-selection agreement on those models. We read this as model-side sensitivity to ill-formed mid-template splices, not a kernel correctness finding. Characterizing the gradient between boundary-aligned and arbitrary splices per model is follow-up work.

Workload coverage.

The deployment (Section 5) covers 8 debug-gym mini_nightmare tasks ×\times 4 seeds ×\times 2 policies at a single truncation threshold on one model. We do not characterize how the gains depend jointly on policy aggressiveness across thresholds, benchmark family (SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2023), web-research, longer-horizon workloads), model capability, trajectory-divergence behavior, or eviction aggressiveness. Mapping the surface is deferred to follow-up work, and the mechanism contribution does not depend on which cell wins.

Composed mechanism ×\times policy ablation.

The mechanism leg of the validation runs on synthetic prompts (Appendix B); the policy leg runs on debug-gym under the standard re-prefill arm (Section 5). The composed ablation that would attribute the deployment win between the two contributions, namely running the splice arm against the same truncation policy on the same debug-gym tasks, is the natural next step. Exercising the splice path through the agent’s per-turn message-edit flow rather than through the controlled microbench of Appendix B is engineering on the agent–serving seam, not a Leyline-design gap. Section 4 predicts the splice arm would preserve original-chunk context that the re-prefill arm loses, and we expect this to manifest as a different (likely smaller) per-step context-cleanup magnitude under splice than under re-prefill.

Empirical-coverage scope.

Appendices E, F, and G cover the corner cases we identified as load-bearing: varied span sizes (8–200 tokens), 1–2 non-overlapping edits per turn, positive and negative Δ\Delta, two stub-content modes, chained rotations up to N=100N{=}100 on the same logical slot, and 50-step trajectories with up to 8 edits per turn. The randomized suite uses a single base prompt (counter step 4) per model and 40 trials per cell; widening to multiple base prompts would tighten confidence intervals but is unlikely to change the qualitative picture. The contract’s full-vs-rp prediction is most cleanly testable on Moonlight (where the two references diverge with non-trivial frequency); a broader suite spanning more diverging-reference-frequent models is follow-up work.

Determinism controls.

All replays in Section 4 use greedy decoding (argmax, no sampling, no temperature) over bf16 model weights loaded via stock HuggingFace forward passes (no fused custom kernels, no cudnn-deterministic flag). The full/re-prefill/Leyline paths share identical model state and tokenizer state on each step. We have not measured whether residual bf16 nondeterminism (matmul-reduction ordering on H100 tensor cores) explains any portion of the observed per-step disagreements; the magnitude of cross-path divergence we observe (mean common-prefix lengths far from 128 on GLM-4.7-Flash) far exceeds plausible bf16 reduction noise, so we attribute the disagreements primarily to cached-KV sensitivity, not floating-point reordering.

bf16 K-storage precision floor.

Distinct from matmul-reduction nondeterminism, the bf16 KV pool imposes a structural per-K-entry precision floor of ∼\sim1–3% (uniform across rotation positions; measured in App. Q). Argmax flips happen on the small fraction of prompts (∼\sim4% on our long-context replay) whose top-1 vs top-2 logit gap is smaller than that noise. The current mitigation (AKASHA_PIC_ROTATION_FP32=1, default on) removes the rotation computation’s contribution by running the cos/sin multiply in fp32; the rotation storage (the bf16 KV pool itself) remains the floor. Workloads that require byte-identical outputs to a full prefill on every prompt would need either higher-precision K storage or an argmax-margin gate before committing a splice. Workloads that tolerate sampling-noise-scale token differences (chat, long agentic loops where individual token choice is not load-bearing) are unaffected.

Cold-start coverage and warm-start scope.

The manifest warm-start mechanism (Section 5, App. S) bypasses the within-batch peer-discovery race only for content the manifest covers, and we have demonstrated its activation in the narrow 2-tenant C=4C{=}4 configuration. Tenant-count sweep ({3,4,8}\{3,4,8\} tenants at C=4C{=}4) and concurrency extension (C=8C{=}8 at 2 tenants with warm-start) all reach cand_total=0{=}0 even though the registry shows 1515–3535 unique observed hashes (jobs 473946473946–473952473952, App. U). The candidate filter rejects the warmup-time inserts once the live workload’s first batch reaches match_prefix, consistent with the warmup request’s pool slots having been freed by then. The directive contract (Section 4) is independent of this filter behavior; closing it is concrete engineering (separate warmup process, or persistent fetchable representation in the registry) and not on the critical path of the design.

KV-pool occupancy is not the figure of merit.

The savings reported in Section 5 are re-prefill compute and pool writes avoided, not concurrent allocator memory. Role B inserts spliced chunks into the radix trie by reference, so the spliced slots remain trie-pinned and the allocator’s peak available_size() does not drop. The 4-tenant measurement (App. U) shows splice-ON and splice-OFF peaks identical to the slot (97.597.5 MB), and the 2-tenant ON + warm-start peak is +12+12 MB above OFF (from the four warm-up-preloaded articles staying pinned). The matched-configuration tenant slope at concurrency C=4C{=}4 is 1.82×1.82\times (splice OFF, 2-tenant →\to 4-tenant) vs 1.71×1.71\times (splice ON + warm-start, same range; the 4-tenant arm of that pair produces no spliced chunks, so the slope reduction beyond the splice-OFF baseline is from warm-start pinning rather than splice activity at 4-tenant). Read together, the splice’s chunk-level overlap detection produces a measurable but modest tenant-scaling-slope reduction (the linear projection is 2.0×2.0\times). Deployments whose memory constraint is peak allocator pressure cannot rely on the splice to drop their watermark; deployments whose constraint is prefill compute under high cross-tenant overlap will see the savings as re-prefill ms not spent.

Logit-level vs token-level equality.

The headline metrics in Tables 4 and 5 are token-level (argmax agreement, common-prefix length, parsed tool-name agreement); Appendix I additionally reports per-step logit-level ℓ2\ell_{2} and KL distances between Leyline and the two reference paths on the counter trajectory for all four models. The picture is consistent with argmax: on edit steps where argmax matches, the per-step KL between Leyline and the matched reference is below 0.5 nats; the bulk distribution can still differ on dimensions far from the top, but the rank-1 token is preserved. A logit-level acceptance test for sampling regimes (rather than greedy) would tighten the empirical contract further and is a natural extension.

Open corner cases for pin-style directives.

A deployed PIN-style directive must answer two engineering questions raised in the vLLM RFC thread (vLLM Project contributors, 2024): resource contention under user-issued pins, and cross-tenant prefix-cache leakage. The directive abstraction is correct independently of either answer (it splices what the policy says to splice); both are deploy-side policy work.
