Appendix A Deployment-cell setup and methodology details

This appendix expands the setup, methodology, and provenance details supporting the deployment-cell evidence reported in Section 5 (Table 2).

Setup.

debug-gym mini_nightmare (Yuan et al., 2025) (eight Python-debugging tasks under hidden-test scoring; the per-task breakdown is in Table 2; pandas_dataframe excluded per Section 5); JoyAI-LLM Flash (Cai et al., 2026) on H200 TP=4 via SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) with the Leyline-integrated RadixCache; two policy classes (truncate_older_than:n=2,max_chars=200 as treatment, keep_all as baseline) at 4 seeds per cell, N=32N{=}32 baseline + 3333 treatment reliable trials (counter has one additional treatment trial; the 31 cells with both arms run anchor the paired analysis), max=50 agent steps per task. The treatment policy truncates tool messages older than 2 turns to a 200-character head/tail stub; Leyline computes the corresponding directive and applies the splice via δ\delta-rotation per Section 3.2. The two policies are exercised through the same re-prefill arm of Section 4.1 (standard radix-cache prefix matching plus re-prefill of the changed suffix), so the observed difference attributes solely to policy behavior at the message-edit interface, not to any splice contribution at the KV-slot layer.

Provenance: policy-loaded check.

All 64 trials carry policy_loaded=1 in their per-trial metadata. This check was added after a fix to the SLURM harness on 2026-05-26 that resolved an unexported MEMOKEEPER_ROOT environment variable in earlier pilots; the post-fix runs reported here are the policy-applied evaluation, and the provenance flag is the harness-level confirmation that the intended truncation policy was active in every cell.

What this evidence shows about the primitive.

Three observations frame what Section 5 establishes about the directive abstraction itself. (i) A 10-line Python policy class produces a stream of (sstart,send,R)(s_{\mathrm{start}},s_{\mathrm{end}},R) tuples consumed cleanly by the policy hook with no per-policy serving-side code, operationalizing the signal-agnosticism property (Section 3). (ii) The integration runs end-to-end on SGLang + debug-gym + JoyAI-LLM Flash with no friction at the agent-policy interface. (iii) Under the message-edit regime, the radix prefix matches across consecutive turns on every prefix-stable directive, realizing the cache-friendliness property at the message-list level (the same property the splice mechanism realizes at the KV-slot level inside the kernel). Scope limits are catalogued in Limitations.

Appendix B Three-arm message-edit microbenchmark

Section 5 reports the policy leg of the two-leg validation under the standard re-prefill arm; this appendix reports the mechanism leg by isolating the splice kernel’s contribution under controlled prompts. We run a three-arm microbenchmark against the live SGLang scheduler on DeepSeek-V2-Lite (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2024a) (and JoyAI-LLM Flash; see end of section) with the same workload across all three arms:

  • •

    cache-off: SGLang with --disable-radix-cache — every request re-prefills from scratch. Lower bound on what the splice mechanism can possibly beat.

  • •

    radix: vanilla SGLang with its default radix cache. The serving-stack baseline an agentic harness already gets for free; matches the unchanged conversation prefix up to the edit point but not past it.

  • •

    splice: Leyline’s directive-driven splice path active in the same SGLang process via a content-hash + δ\delta-rotation hook in the radix-match path (the in-place mechanism of Section 3.2). The arm under test.

Workload.

Each session is a multi-theme synthetic conversation (cooking / programming / history / science) with a long system prompt (≈4096\approx 4096 tokens) and six user turns of ≈2048\approx 2048 tokens each, constructed from topic words slotted into a fixed template family (“How do I get the consistency of risotto right when I’m a beginner?”). Total prompt length at the final turn reaches ≈17\approx 17 K tokens. We run the same three-phase trace as the synthetic message-edit pattern of prior work:

  1. 1.

    Build: issue turns 1 through KK incrementally, populating the radix cache (and, on the splice arm, the content-hash registry) with the original conversation prefix.

  2. 2.

    Edit: re-issue the conversation up to the edit turn with the topic word swapped for a same-template synonym (“risotto” →\rightarrow “paella”). The surrounding template tokens are byte-identical to the original, so the post-edit turns tedit+1,…,tKt_{\mathrm{edit}+1},\ldots,t_{K} are content-identical to the build phase — only shifted in absolute position by Δ=|teditedit|−|teditorig|\Delta=|t_{\mathrm{edit}}^{\mathrm{edit}}|-|t_{\mathrm{edit}}^{\mathrm{orig}}|.

  3. 3.

    Replay: issue the full edited conversation as one POST. This is the message-edit re-prefill case: the radix path matches the unchanged system prompt and the pre-edit turns; everything past the edit must be re-prefilled. The splice path additionally content-hash-matches the shifted-but-identical post-edit turns and rotates their cached KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} by Δ\Delta.

Decoding is greedy (T=0T{=}0) so the three arms are expected to agree token-for-token on the replay phase when the splice path is correctness-preserving — the same contract validated at single-prompt scale in Section 4.

Cross-arm output equivalence — production-scale correctness check across the batch-scaling sweep.

Across the four-cell concurrency sweep we run the post-hoc cross-arm aggregator on the leading 1616 decoded tokens of every request (128128 phase-keyed records per cell, joined by (phase,session,turn,order)(\textsc{phase},\textsc{session},\textsc{turn},\textsc{order})). The splice arm matches the radix arm on first-token argmax in 100%/97.7%/98.4%/94.5%100\%/97.7\%/98.4\%/94.5\% of records at C∈{1,4,8,16}C{\in}\{1,4,8,16\} and on the full 1616-token head in 99.2%/95.3%/93.0%/67.2%99.2\%/95.3\%/93.0\%/67.2\%. The reference disagreement floor — cache-off vs. radix, two arms that share no directive code path — shows the same degradation pattern across concurrencies (97.7%/97.7%/97.7%/94.5%97.7\%/97.7\%/97.7\%/94.5\% first-token; 85.2%/93.8%/90.6%/68.8%85.2\%/93.8\%/90.6\%/68.8\% full head), confirming the splice-vs-radix disagreement is scheduler-induced bf16-reduction noise (matmul-reduction ordering on H100 tensor cores reorders under batching, see Numerics.), not a directive-layer correctness gap. The splice path tracks the warm-prefix path at the noise floor of batched scheduling — the production-scale analogue of the single-prompt argmax claim in Table 4.

Result — splice arm produces a uniform +11.2\boldsymbol{+11.2} pp cache-hit gain across the 𝑪=𝟏→𝟏𝟔\boldsymbol{C{=}1{\to}16} batch-scaling sweep, with peak e2e latency win at 𝑪=𝟖\boldsymbol{C{=}8}.

Table 3 reports the four-cell batch-scaling sweep. The replay cache-hit ratio is invariant across concurrency: cache-off 0.0%0.0\%, standard radix 49.6%49.6\%, Leyline splice 60.8%\mathbf{60.8\%} (+11.2+11.2 pp uniformly at C∈{1,4,8,16}C\in\{1,4,8,16\}). The splice mechanism’s correctness property holds across the entire batch range. The e2e latency win is non-monotonic: −51-51 ms at C=1C{=}1, −85-85 ms at C=4C{=}4, −𝟐𝟒𝟏\mathbf{-241} ms (−4.4%\mathbf{-4.4\%}) at C=8C{=}8, and +45+45 ms (within scheduler noise) at C=16C{=}16. The peak at C=8C{=}8 matches the prediction that splice gains compound when prefill contention is high relative to the decode tail; at C=1C{=}1 the splice saves prefill compute that runs in serial with decode, producing a smaller absolute win; at C=16C{=}16 the saved prefill compute is absorbed into the now decode-dominated tail and stops moving the p50 needle, though the splice still produces 203203 chunk hits worth of saved compute (re-issued in the next request batch). Per-cell PIC counters: chunks_spliced ∈{167,203}\in\{167,203\} (lower in the C=4C{=}4 cell where four sessions partially serialize through the splice path’s lookup); cumulative bytes_rotated ≥740\geq 740 MB; cumulative in-place rotation-kernel time ≤2.9\leq 2.9 ms per run (negligible against the multi-second e2e). The build and edit phases show the splice and radix arms at identical cache-hit ratios because the splice mechanism only activates on replay (where the message-edit pattern produces shifted-but-identical content); this matches the directive contract’s prediction in Section 3.1.

Tail-latency (p99) corroborates the p50 picture at the peak and exposes a localized rotation-contention outlier at low CC.

The replay-phase p99 e2e tracks the p50 story at the headline cell: at C=8C{=}8 the splice arm reaches 52985298 ms p99 against radix’s 55435543 ms p99 (−245-245 ms, −4.4%-4.4\%), and the radix-vs-splice gap is consistent at p50/p90/p99. At C=1C{=}1 and C=4C{=}4 the splice arm produces a mild tail spike — one or two requests per cell hit p99 ≈5300\approx 5300 ms vs radix’s ≈4100\approx 4100–47404740 ms p99 — which we attribute to the first-time rotation walk on a cold registry (the chunk-content hash takes a microsecond-scale extra walk on the very first match, amortizing across subsequent requests; the chunker’s CDC pass on a ≥17\geq 17 K-token prompt accounts for the variability). At C=16C{=}16 the splice arm matches radix on p99 (72187218 ms vs 71717171 ms, within noise). The headline cell (C=8C{=}8) is the deployment-relevant one for production agentic serving — a single H100 typically runs more than one session concurrently — and the splice arm beats radix on every percentile reported.

What unlocks the gain across the entire batch range.

Three workload-and-stack properties together make the splice arm exceed radix at every concurrency: (i) the post-edit suffix is large enough (≥4\geq 4 turn-pairs of ≈2\approx 2 K tokens ≈8\approx 8 K tokens) that the CDC chunker’s Gear-hash rolling signature has multiple opportunities to find a boundary aligned with a previously registered chunk’s boundary; (ii) AKASHA_PIC_ABSPOS_CDC=1 stabilizes chunk hashes across requests that share content but have differing radix-match prefixes, so registered chunks remain findable on the replay-phase prompt; (iii) the A1 anchored CDC variant of the chunker (activated via AKASHA_PIC_ANCHOR_CDC=1; the production default in the runs above) forces a CDC boundary AND resets the rolling hash at chat-template special tokens auto-extracted from the tokenizer at model-runner init. (iii) is the load-bearing fix at concurrency >1>1: without it, the registry-side content-hash match rate at C=16C{=}16 collapses to zero (cf. the documented cand_local/noncontig_chunks_skipped regression on the unanchored chunker that motivated A1). With (iii) active, cand_local climbs to 128128–203203 matches at every concurrency tested. None of (i)–(iii) is bespoke to this workload; they describe what an agentic workload at production scale would naturally exhibit once the chunker is chat-template-aware.

What the (then) small-prompt negative isolated, and the anchored-CDC fix that closed it.

An earlier sweep at Lsys=512L_{\mathrm{sys}}{=}512, Lturn=256L_{\mathrm{turn}}{=}256, Lout=64L_{\mathrm{out}}{=}64, with the legacy purely-Gear-hash chunker (i.e. AKASHA_PIC_ANCHOR_CDC unset), produced 00 chunks_spliced despite the splice path firing ∼56\sim 56 times per session: break_first_chunk_hash_miss incremented on every loop_entered. The diagnosis was that at small workload scale the Gear-hash rolling-window state past the radix-match boundary differs too sharply between BUILD and REPLAY for the chunker to converge on the same boundaries; the chunks of the byte-identical-but-shifted post-edit suffix are then never registered under matching content hashes. We characterized this as a localized chunking-strategy gap forward-compatible with the directive contract and identified the chat-template-anchored chunker as the natural fix; that fix has since landed in the underlying Akasha stack as the A1 anchored CDC chunker (env: AKASHA_PIC_ANCHOR_CDC=1), is the active configuration in all four runs of Table 3, and is the load-bearing mechanism for the uniform +11.2+11.2 pp gain across concurrencies C∈{1,4,8,16}C\in\{1,4,8,16\} above. The kernel and directive contract are unchanged; the change is purely in how the chunker selects boundaries.

Scope and what this section does and does not show.

The microbenchmark validates that Leyline’s serving-stack integration (sitecustomize-driven monkey-patch of Req.init_next_round_input, Scheduler._add_request_to_queue, and ModelRunner.__init__; rotary-emb stash; splice_at_match hook into the radix-cache match path; byte-counter instrumentation through the rotation kernel; chat-template-anchored CDC) is live in a production SGLang scheduler and produces a uniform +11.2+11.2 pp replay-cache-hit improvement over the standard radix baseline across concurrencies C∈{1,4,8,16}C\in\{1,4,8,16\} at production-scale prompts (≈17\approx 17 K tokens), with the e2e win peaking at −241-241 ms (−4.4%-4.4\%) at C=8C{=}8. It does not characterize how the splice gain compounds across mixed workload profiles (heavy-tail per-session prompt sizes, variable edit-rates), under HiCache/disk-tier prefix-cache stacks, or under multi-tenant request routing; those extensions are deployment-side follow-up. The constructed single-prompt microbenchmark of Section 4.1 establishes that the kernel correctness contract holds under in-place splice; this section establishes that the production-scheduler integration of that kernel is mechanically alive, produces a measurable cache-hit gain at every concurrency tested, and the chunker-side small-prompt regression is closed by the anchored-CDC fix described above.

Appendix C Kernel specification: tensors and composition

Step-by-step tensor effect of one directive.

A directive’s kernel effect on the cache is fully specified by four operations on three regions of the cache layout. (a) The evicted span’s slots [sstart,send)[s_{\mathrm{start}},s_{\mathrm{end}}) are freed: KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}}, KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}}, and VV at those positions are released back to the KV-pool allocator. (b) The replacement RR is freshly prefilled into newly allocated slots at positions [sstart,sstart+|R|)[s_{\mathrm{start}},s_{\mathrm{start}}+|R|), computing K and VV for these tokens against the cache prefix up to sstarts_{\mathrm{start}} via a normal forward pass. (c) Downstream slots originally at positions i≥sendi\geq s_{\mathrm{end}} have only their KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} rotated by Δ\Delta (Equation 1) and are re-keyed in the radix structure to occupy logical positions i+Δi+\Delta; their KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}} and VV are untouched. (d) No Q tensor is cached for the decode path (Q is recomputed each step from current hidden states), so no Q reindexing is required. Sink tokens (the first NN tokens for streaming-attention-style sinks) are unaffected provided sstart>Ns_{\mathrm{start}}>N; deployments that violate this can either widen sstarts_{\mathrm{start}} or treat the sink prefix as pinned. We rule out layernorm and attention-sink interactions as confounders by validating bit-identity in the no-edit case (Section 4) and by the closed-form rotation-algebra argument in Section 3.2.

Multiple directives, overlapping spans, signed Δ\Delta.

A turn may carry multiple directives. We require non-overlapping spans at the directive layer (an overlapping submission is rejected at apply-time; merging two adjacent removals is the policy’s responsibility, not the kernel’s). Within one turn the kernel processes directives left-to-right with the running position shift carried over: a directive at sstart,2s_{\mathrm{start},2} applied after one with shift Δ1\Delta_{1} sees the downstream slots at their already-shifted positions i+Δ1i+\Delta_{1}, and the rotation algebra closes under composition (R⁡(Δ1)​R​(Δ2)=R⁡(Δ1+Δ2)R(\Delta_{1})R(\Delta_{2})=R(\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}), so re-rotating an already-rotated slot is well-defined). Δ\Delta may be positive (replacement longer than the evicted span; downstream tokens shift right; new slots are allocated) or negative (the common case: replacement shorter; downstream tokens shift left; freed slots are released after the rotation). The radix invariant maintained across both signs is: for every cached prefix the path from root to leaf encodes a contiguous, position-monotonic sequence of slot pointers with KK/VV consistent with the prompt that produced them under the contract of Section 3.1. Holes (positions deallocated by negative Δ\Delta but not yet reclaimed by the allocator) are normal radix bookkeeping handled by the existing allocator.

Appendix D Cross-architecture counter-trajectory replay

The primitive runs unmodified on four MLA-family open-weight models: DeepSeek-V2-Lite (16B) (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2024a), JoyAI-LLM Flash (DSv3-derivative, 48B/3B) (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2024b; Cai et al., 2026), GLM-4.7-Flash (Team GLM and others, 2024), and Moonlight-16B-A3B (Moonshot AI, 2025). The replay is a 12-step counter trajectory with a 128-token greedy decode at each step; six of the twelve steps involve a directive edit (the policy’s truncation horizon takes effect once enough turn history has accumulated; the first six steps have no edits). No per-model code; the same rotation kernel; the same directive interface. We report per-model metrics: (i) tool-name agreement on edit steps where both the directive-active and full-context paths emit a parseable tool call within the 128-token decode (denominator: number of such “both-parseable” steps out of 6 edit steps); (ii) first-token argmax agreement against the full-context baseline (the contract from Section 3.1) and (iii) against the re-prefill-of-edited-prompt path (a stricter reference Leyline does not promise); (iv) mean common-prefix length between the directive-active decode and each reference.

The JoyAI, DSv2-Lite, and Moonlight configurations overlap with Irminsul’s cross-architecture validation (Ma et al., 2026); GLM-4.7-Flash is added here. On the 6 edit steps the JoyAI run shows first-token agreement with both references on 3/63/6 (the three paths converge or diverge together at the first-token level on this trajectory); on the other 33 edit steps Leyline emits an extra block of reasoning text where the full-context path emits a tool call directly. Full 128-token strings match on 2/62/6 edit steps; mean common-prefix length is 41.841.8 tokens against both references (rounded to 4242 in Table 4). On GLM the mean common-prefix length against rp (9.79.7, table 1010) marginally exceeds that against full (6.26.2, table 66); both are short because GLM’s first-token disagreement diverges the suffix early in the decode, and the 33-token gap is incidental given the per-trajectory references agree on every edit-step first token (see caption to Table 4).

Appendix E Randomized edit-suite stress test

The replay setups in Section 4.1 and Appendix D use policy-derived edits: span sizes are whatever the truncation policy produces, Δ\Delta is always negative (truncation only), and each turn contains at most one edit. To probe corner cases this distribution misses — positive Δ\Delta (insertion), wider span-size range, multiple non-overlapping edits per turn — we run a synthetic random-edit harness against the same kernel as the replay path. Each trial samples (i) k∈{1,2}k\in\{1,2\} non-overlapping spans from the same base prompt (step 4 of the counter trajectory, L≈3200L\approx 3200 tokens after chat templating); (ii) each span’s size uniformly in [8,200][8,200] tokens at a position uniformly inside the prompt’s body; (iii) each replacement length uniformly in [0,2⋅|span|][0,2{\cdot}|\mathrm{span}|], so Δ\Delta ranges over both signs. The kernel splices the sampled directives in a single call alongside a substituted-prompt re-prefill for comparison. We report on 40 trials per model per stub mode.

The four-model picture together with the random-vs-semantic comparison gives the honest version of the contract story. DSv2-Lite is invariant: no trial produces a first-token divergence under either stub mode, so the contract’s full-vs-rp prediction is vacuous (consistent with Table 4 and the bit-identical stub ablation in Appendix M). Moonlight is the model on which the prediction is cleanly testable: 1313–1717 trials produce diverging references and Leyline tracks full-context on 1111–1414 of them, re-prefill on 00, with the remainder matching neither — consistent with the positional contract (Section 3.1) across both stub modes.

JoyAI and GLM behave more brittly under both random-position stub modes: Leyline produces a first token that matches neither reference on 2020–36/4036/40 trials, and never matches the full-context reference exclusively. The random↔\leftrightarrowsemantic comparison rules out stub content as the discriminator: switching from random-in-vocab tokens to a fixed placeholder string changes the rates only slightly (e.g. JoyAI “matches neither” goes 30→2030{\to}20/4040, GLM stays 33→3633{\to}36/4040). The discriminator versus Table 4 — where the same kernel on JoyAI hits 4/44/4 parsed tool-name agreement and 3/63/6 first-token agreement — is edit position: the random-edit harness splices at uniform-random token offsets inside the chat-rendered prompt body, frequently cutting across chat-template structure (mid-message, mid-tool-tag, between role markers), whereas the policy-derived runs splice at chat-message boundaries the model expects to be edited. We document this as a model-side sensitivity to ill-formed prompt structure, not a kernel correctness finding — the deployment-relevant policies (turn-window truncation, span-aligned eviction, summarization-into-stub) splice at message boundaries by construction. The 1818–2929 positive-Δ\Delta trials per row and 1919–2121 multi-edit-per-turn trials per row exercise the composition closure in Section 3.3 and the signed-Δ\Delta allocator behavior; the patterns above apply uniformly across single-edit/multi-edit and positive/negative Δ\Delta subsets.

Appendix F Chained-rotation drift in bf16

The composition closure R⁡(a)​R​(b)=R⁡(a+b)R(a)R(b)=R(a+b) holds in exact arithmetic, so chained rotations should be mathematically equivalent to a single rotation by the sum. Under bf16 we ask whether per-rotation round-off accumulates. We test at the kernel level on synthetic K vectors, comparing NN chained random-delta rotations against (a) a single equivalent-sum rotation, and (b) the fresh-RoPE-at-target-position reference. Each NN uses 1010 seeds; deltas sampled in [−512,+512][-512,+512] with the running position constrained to the cache range. K vectors are bf16 of shape [batch=8,heads=32,head​_​dim=64][\mathrm{batch}{=}8,\mathrm{heads}{=}32,\mathrm{head\_dim}{=}64].

Rel-L2 drift grows from 4.3×10−34.3{\times}10^{-3} at N=2N{=}2 to 2.6×10−22.6{\times}10^{-2} at N=100N{=}100, a 6.1×6.1{\times} growth across a 50×50{\times} rotation-count increase — sub-linear in NN, consistent with random-walk noise accumulation. Workloads where the same physical slot is re-rotated more than ∼100{\sim}100 times — e.g. very-long-horizon agentic sessions with hundreds of edits targeting positions downstream of the same persistent prefix — would benefit from periodic re-prefill of the affected slots; we document this as a deployment guideline (Numerics.) rather than a correctness gap.

Appendix G Long-horizon trajectory replay

The counter trajectory of Appendix D has 12 steps with 6 edit steps; deployment scenarios commonly run much longer (debug-gym’s sum_tree problems regularly produce 50-step trajectories (Yuan et al., 2025)). We replay a 50-step sum_tree trajectory through each of the four MLA models with the same truncation policy as the counter case, separating per-turn-edit counts (the policy’s truncation horizon means later turns truncate more older messages: up to 8 edits per turn by step 50). Table 7 reports first-token agreement against the full-context baseline, split between single-edit-per-turn and multi-edit-per-turn subsets.

The single- vs multi-edit split is informative. DSv2-Lite is robust on both subsets even with up to 8 simultaneous edits at L∼28​K{\sim}28\mathrm{K} tokens. GLM-4.7-Flash holds ≥ 80%{\geq}\,80\% on both; the multi-edit subset is slightly higher than single, which we attribute to the later-trajectory stubs being well-rehearsed by the model. Moonlight-16B-A3B is the case where long-horizon trajectory replay degrades on tokens: first-token agreement drops to ∼56%{\sim}56\% on single-edit turns at sum_tree’s later steps. JoyAI-LLM Flash degrades further — 12%12\% single-edit and 4%4\% multi-edit token agreement at L∼28​K{\sim}28\mathrm{K}. The full and re-prefill references on JoyAI agree on first-token 82%82\% of the time and on extracted tool name 42/43=98%42/43{=}98\%; Leyline tracks the references at 67%67\% (single-edit) and 72%72\% (multi-edit) on tool-name under a permissive multi-format parser, while diverging at token granularity. We do not attribute this to chained-rotation drift (App. F shows sub-linear growth up to N=100N{=}100); the more likely explanation is the same model-side sensitivity to ill-formed mid-template content observed in Table 5, manifesting on a long-prompt-length axis: JoyAI alternates between JSON-list and XML <tool_call> output formats turn-by-turn, and small KV perturbations flip which format the model emits even when the tool choice is preserved.

Appendix J Programmable memory verbs beyond splice

This appendix elaborates the four verbs sketched in Section 7. The directive abstraction is the same; each verb names a distinct semantic intent the agent can declare and the kernel can execute. Experimental validation of each is future work.

Lifecycle hints: DECAY for tool-call chains.

Multi-step agent workflows have well-defined utility horizons. In a read →\to analyze →\to write pipeline, the KV entries for file contents retrieved during read are no longer needed once analyze completes. A semantic DECAY directive issued at the boundary of analyze tells the storage layer to deprioritize these entries proactively (e.g., compress and migrate to CPU), freeing GPU capacity for write without waiting for end-of-request eviction. The agent knows the phase boundary; no system-side predictor does.

Span isolation: EVICT for reasoning traces and failed tool calls.

Reasoning models emit extended internal monologues (within <think> spans) that are semantically inert to the final output. Under standard serving, these KV entries persist until request completion. A semantic EVICT directive at the closing tag enables immediate reclamation, reducing peak memory pressure during long-horizon tasks. This is the canonical splice operation that this paper validates, applied at a span boundary the agent can identify exactly.

A second instance arises naturally in agentic coding: when a str replace style edit tool call fails because the old_str string does not match the current file state, the model retries with a corrected call. Once the corrected call succeeds, the KV span covering the failed attempt — the original old_str/new_str pair, any interleaved reasoning, and the error response — is semantically dead: it records an action the agent has superseded. An EVICT directive emitted alongside the successful retry reclaims this span immediately. The agent possesses the reliable signal (it knows the retry succeeded); the storage layer does not.

Hard retention: PIN for deterministic prefetch.

Speculative tool-execution work (Nichols et al., 2025) prefetches predicted future tool calls during generation, reducing end-to-end latency but wasting work on mispredictions. A semantic PIN directive provides a complementary mechanism: when an agent explicitly declares “the span I am about to emit will be needed in the next turn,” the storage layer can treat this as a hard retention guarantee rather than a probabilistic estimate, converting speculation into deterministic prefetch. The block-level Pin in LMCache is the storage-side enforcement; the semantic PIN is the agent-side declaration that produces it. Industry deployments are converging on related designs: analysis of Claude Code’s internals describes a speculative-execution subsystem that pre-runs predicted commands in an isolated sandbox before user confirmation (Spano, 2026), indicating that agent–serving co-design around execution prediction is already a practical concern.

Attention-mask isolation: SCRATCH.

A natural extension is scratchpad KV — context that participates in attention during a reasoning step but is excluded from the output stream and reclaimed immediately on span completion. This requires attention-mask-level isolation beyond the current splice vocabulary and beyond LMCache’s block-level Compress, but the directive interface offers a clean extension point: a SCRATCH annotation could instruct the kernel to apply the appropriate mask and reclaim entries at span close. The mask-level mechanism is not in this paper; the interface space that admits it is.

Cross-session sharing: SHARE(scope, placement_hint).

The four verbs above describe intra-session, intra-agent KV lifecycle. A fifth verb extends the vocabulary across the session boundary: scope∈{session,user_group,global}\textit{scope}\in\{\textit{session},\textit{user\_group},\textit{global}\} and placement_hint∈{local,rank_k,replicated}\textit{placement\_hint}\in\{\textit{local},\textit{rank\_k},\textit{replicated}\}. SHARE differs from PIN: PIN prevents eviction for the current agent; SHARE declares “make this chunk available to other agents.” The two compose: PIN+SHARE is the canonical pattern for a reference codebase served across multiple refactoring agents. The directive abstraction is the right home for this verb because the agent, not the storage layer, knows when a chunk has cross-session intent. The system-side substrate already exists: knowledge-delivery-network architectures (Cheng et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025) supply the storage tier, compute-vs-load tradeoff schedulers (Jin et al., 2024) the orchestration, RAG-specific shared caches (Lee et al., 2025) the persistence layer, multi-tenant KV reuse systems (Yang et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024) the cross-instance migration. The closest naming overlaps come from adjacent layers: LMCache exposes operator-side pin/unpin (Liu et al., 2025) (system-orchestration vocabulary, not agent-emitted), and Anthropic’s cache_control (Anthropic, 2024) is agent-emitted but single-tenant, single-prefix, and stands alone rather than sitting in a vocabulary. The empirical validation, threat model (cross-tenant prefix-cache leakage in particular), and provider-curated deployment are the subject of follow-up work.

Appendix K Composition with concurrent and adjacent work

Concurrent signal-side work.

The signal-side contributions of SideQuest (Kariyappa and Suh, 2026) (learned semantic-utility detector) and LoopGuard (Xu et al., 2026) (decoder-side degeneration detection) compose naturally with Leyline: any signal expressible as a span-set to evict can drive a Leyline directive without retraining the kernel or the signal detector. The right division of labor in the agentic-LLM stack is signal source in one paper, mechanism abstraction in another.

Active-RAG.

FLARE (Jiang et al., 2023) and Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) promise uncertainty-triggered retrieval mid-generation, but in production stumble on two coupled obstacles: calibration breakdown in RLHF-trained models, which makes the uncertainty trigger unreliable; and position-encoding invalidation when retrieved content is spliced into a live cache, which forces a re-prefill on every injection. CacheBlend (Yao et al., 2024) addresses the second obstacle on MHA via selective cross-attention recomputation; for MLA, the position-invariant cKVc_{\mathrm{KV}} channel plus the δ\delta-rotation of Ma et al. (2026) provides a structurally cheaper resolution. Leyline’s directive interface makes the first obstacle tractable by separating the uncertainty oracle (an external policy that decides when to retrieve and what to inject) from the cache-edit mechanism (the directive that splices without re-prefill). The result is a clean division of labor across the stack: an external oracle supplies policy; the directive supplies the semantic edit; the storage layer (LMCache (Liu et al., 2025), where deployed) handles the resulting block-level movement across the GPU/CPU/storage hierarchy.

Scope notes.

Two non-claim items from the main text bear restating. First, we do not develop the side observation that Leyline preserves more context than the rendered prompt suggests; that dependence is workload-specific and deserves separate empirical treatment. Second, variation we observe across models is in agent behavior under Leyline-managed cache (signal-policy-workload-dependent), not in whether the directive-driven rotation works.

Appendix L vLLM framework RFC threads

The block-level lifecycle half of the agentic cache problem is now consolidated in production. LMCache (Liu et al., 2025) ships an enterprise-grade control API with Pin, Clear, Move, Compress, and Lookup operating on cache blocks in physical storage tiers, integrated with vLLM and SGLang. vLLM’s internal KVEvents mechanism (consumed by the NVIDIA Dynamo router) covers the introspection side.

The semantic-edit half has not. Four recent vLLM proposals each request a slice of cache control at the layer above the storage backend: [RFC] Pinned Caching (vLLM Project contributors, 2024) asks for manual-expiration directives over the radix cache (a higher-level Pin than LMCache’s block-level Pin); [RFC] KV-Cache Interoperability API (vLLM Project contributors, 2025b) proposes to expose KVEvents as a public contract for external policy consumers; [RFC] Sparse KV Cache Management (vLLM Project contributors, 2025c) sketches a pluggable framework for non-LRU eviction policies; [RFC] Generalized KV Cache Reuse (vLLM Project contributors, 2025a) lifts the prefix-only restriction so non-prefix token subsets can be reused, the necessary precondition for splice. None of these proposals defines a span-level edit operation with the position-encoding correctness story that splicing through the kernel requires; each surfaces a piece of the unsolved layer.

The threads on these four RFCs follow a consistent pattern. The maintainers engage substantively, raise corner cases (resource contention when GPU memory runs out under user-issued pins, cross-user prefix-cache leakage under content-addressed cache, hole-filling under H2O-style sparse eviction), then run out of consensus on the right level of abstraction. The Sparse-KV thread is exemplary: contributors converge on the diagnosis that the framework needs to decouple logical from physical memory management so that the scheduler does not have to know which eviction or offloading policy is in effect, but the discussion ends without a maintainer-accepted abstraction (vLLM Project contributors, 2025c). The same shape recurs in the Generalized-Reuse follow-up: with no cache-layer primitive available, contributors propose a request-batching workaround — splitting one prompt into three (tokens 0--9, 0--19, 0--29), batching with two as placeholders, discarding the placeholder outputs — to recompute holes outside the cache layer entirely (vLLM Project contributors, 2025a).

Leyline’s directive abstraction is the layer this pattern is missing: a single declarative interface in which all four verbs (pin, expose, evict, splice) are well-typed, with one mathematical foundation (the δ\delta-rotation rule) that gives correctness across the vocabulary — and which the kernel applies in place rather than forcing the workaround out to the scheduler layer. The mutation half currently forces deployments into a correctness-versus-reuse tradeoff that Leyline closes.

Appendix M Stub-content invariance ablation

The δ\delta-rotation, not the stub text, is the load-bearing operation. We demonstrate this with a 4×3×24\times 3\times 2 ablation:

  • •

    4 stub modes: faithful (a short human-readable marker), pad (length-matched whitespace), scrambled (length-matched noise), empty (|R|=0|R|{=}0).

  • •

    3 trajectories: counter, shopping_cart, sum_tree from debug-gym mini_nightmare (Yuan et al., 2025).

  • •

    2 models: DeepSeek-V2-Lite (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2024a), JoyAI-LLM Flash (Cai et al., 2026).

On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, all four stub modes produce bit-identical character-level outputs within each trajectory — zero observable variation. On JoyAI-LLM Flash, tool-name agreement holds at ≥0.98\geq 0.98 across all 12 cells.

Practical implication.

Deployments can use |R|=0|R|{=}0 (the empty stub) and reduce prefill cost further without measurable quality change. This complements Irminsul’s stance that content-addressed caching is a first-class primitive: the cache’s correctness is governed by the rotation rule and the radix structure, not by the surface form of intermediate stubs.

Appendix N Forward compatibility across attention-architecture changes

The δ\delta-rotation correctness story applies to DeepSeek V2/V3-class MLA, where the trained model expects RoPE-encoded keys at their original absolute positions and attends densely over the causal range. Two recent DeepSeek releases test the directive abstraction at different points in the attention-architecture design space — one that preserves MLA and adds trained sparsity (V3.2-Exp), and one that replaces MLA outright (V4).

Within-MLA evolution: V3.2-Exp.

DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2025) retains MLA and adds DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA): a learned Lightning Indexer scores each query against MLA’s compressed token representations and the model attends only to the top-kk selected keys per query rather than to a dense window. Two properties carry over from the dense MLA baseline. First, causality is preserved: the indexer selects only from the causal range, and the selected positions remain in their natural causal order. Second, RoPE correctness is per-position: each selected key carries its RoPE encoding at its original absolute position. Sparse attention is a trained-in operation, not a license to feed the model K vectors at arbitrary new positions.

What V3.2-Exp changes for the directive abstraction is the cost of non-splice verbs. PIN- and SHARE-style retention (Appendix J) can be implemented more efficiently when the kernel is sparse-aware: a content-addressed store of pinned spans composes naturally with top-kk selection, and the indexer can be biased to include or exclude particular spans without touching positional encodings. A splice that re-anchors downstream positions still requires the δ\delta-rotation correction or an equivalent, because RoPE correctness applies regardless of which attention pattern — dense or sparse — consumes the keys.

Out-of-MLA evolution: DSv4.

DeepSeek-V4 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) replaces MLA with a Hybrid Attention Architecture: Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA), which compresses the KV cache along the sequence dimension and applies DSA-style top-kk selection, and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA), which applies heavier sequence-dimension compression with dense attention. The cKVc_{\mathrm{KV}}/KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}}/KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}} structure of MLA is no longer present; MLA’s per-position RoPE-on-KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} correctness argument does not transfer to a sequence-compressed representation. Whatever position-correctness story V4 admits (CSA-specific, HCA-specific, or layer-mixed) lives below the directive interface. The directive itself remains well-typed: a span [sstart,send)[s_{\mathrm{start}},s_{\mathrm{end}}) to splice with replacement RR is the same input regardless of how the kernel realizes it. Empirical validation on V4-class architectures is out of scope for this paper.

For the four MLA configurations validated in Appendix D — DeepSeek-V2-Lite, JoyAI-LLM Flash (DSv3-derived), GLM-4.7-Flash, Moonlight-16B-A3B — splice + δ\delta-rotation is the correctness mechanism, and V3.2-Exp inherits it with sparse-aware optimizations available for non-splice verbs. V4 is the case that motivates keeping policy and mechanism on different sides of the directive: the rotation kernel is MLA-specific and will not survive the architecture replacement, but the span-level interface above it does.

Appendix O Discussion notes: governance patterns, release plan, open follow-ups

This appendix expands four items referenced from the Discussion (Section 7): the concrete governance patterns the two-mode directive enables, the open-source release plan, the rotate-only-vs-boundary-recomputation open question, and the concurrency / tenant-isolation guarantees production deployments need on top of the per-request contract.

Governance patterns on top of the mode-declaration contract.

Three patterns follow once the API surface declares m∈{amortize,forget}m\in\{\textsc{amortize},\textsc{forget}\}. (i) Sensitive-content default. A serving stack that receives directives from harnesses handling PII or regulated data should configure the policy hook to mark such spans forget-mode by default and require an opt-in for amortize. (ii) Per-edit auditability. The serving telemetry distinguishes the two modes, so an audit pipeline can answer “which evictions truly erased context vs. amortized it forward” without inspecting the cache. (iii) Reviewer-debugger consistency. A debugger or safety auditor inspecting a conversation transcript needs to know whether displayed-prompt edits are amortize-mode (cache still attends to the original chunk) or forget-mode (cache rebuilt past the edit); the API contract surfaces that distinction rather than burying it in serving-stack defaults. We do not claim these patterns close all governance questions; the two-mode split moves them from “hidden serving-stack behavior” to “declared API contract,” which is what makes them auditable.

Open-source release plan.

The artifacts described in this paper — the MLA KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} rotation kernel, the policy-driven directive API including the amortize/forget mode split, the live SGLang content-hash hook, and the HuggingFace transformers replay path used for Section 4 — will be released under a permissive license on de-anonymization. The release is structured in three layers matching the abstraction stack: a kernel package (rotation primitives, mode-routed splice entry point), a policy SDK (the Policy.transform interface plus the in-process directive scheduler), and an integration shim (SGLang radix-cache patch plus an HF-transformers replay harness for offline correctness). The three-arm message-edit microbenchmark of Appendix B and the constructed-microbench of Section 4.1 are included as reproducer scripts. Subsequent work — vendor / framework-specific adaptations, complementary recomputation strategies under the directive layer (Section 6), and signal-side policies (Appendix K) — should plug in without forking the kernel.

Open question: when rotate-only suffices vs. when boundary recomputation is needed.

The empirical picture of Sections 6, D and E is gradiated: on MLA models with well-separated KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}}/KnopeK_{\mathrm{nope}} the splice path tracks the full-context reference cleanly at chunk-boundary-aligned edits; under position-arbitrary splices (mid-template) some models exhibit attention shifts away from the rotated suffix that look like the chunk-boundary effects EPIC documents at the reuse boundary (Hu et al., 2025). We hypothesize the relevant architectural cues are (a) the degree to which K dimensions co-encode content and position (full in GQA/MHA, partial-K in MLA), (b) the attention-sink strength at the chunk-start position (stronger sinks make the rotated suffix more sensitive to boundary mismatch), and (c) the rope frequency band the rotation crosses for typical |Δ||\Delta| in the workload. A lightweight runtime detector — decode the first rotated-suffix token under both rotate-only and rotate+kk-recompute, and select whichever matches the full-context reference at higher confidence — is implementable in the existing kernel and is the natural follow-up. The directive layer is unchanged in either case.

Concurrency, batching, and tenant isolation.

The Section 3.3 pipeline is described per-request; production deployments need three additional guarantees. (i) Per-request transactionality of multi-directive turns. A turn carrying kk directives must commit all or none. The kernel applies them left-to-right and the rotation algebra closes under composition (R⁡(Δ1)​R​(Δ2)=R⁡(Δ1+Δ2)R(\Delta_{1})R(\Delta_{2}){=}R(\Delta_{1}{+}\Delta_{2})), but the radix update should be a single transaction so a partial failure rolls back to the pre-turn cache state. This matches existing SGLang scheduler semantics; the directive layer adds no new atomicity requirement beyond what the underlying radix-cache writeback already provides. (ii) Cross-tenant isolation under shared prefixes. When tenants share a prompt prefix in the radix tree, a directive issued by tenant AA at a position downstream of the shared subtree must not affect tenant BB’s view of the cache. Leyline’s implementation routes each directive through the tenant-scoped allocator that already owns the slot range past the shared prefix; the rotation operates on the local (per-tenant) copy of KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} and never touches the shared subtree. Concretely the reference cache carries a per-chunk ChunkEntry.tenant_tag field with cross-tenant filter on splice candidate selection; default tenant_tag=None is the shared-pool opt-in (behaviorally identical to the pre-tenancy baseline), and activation is per-request (operator sets req._akasha_tenant_tag from request headers), so per-tenant resource accounting composes with the splice mechanism without a kernel-level change. (iii) Pinned segments. The PIN verb of Section 7 interacts with the cross-tenant case (does a pinned tenant-AA segment block tenant-BB from reclaiming allocator budget?); the vLLM RFC thread on pinned caching identifies this as a deploy-side policy question rather than a kernel correctness question (App. L). The directive layer expresses both the edit and the per-tenant scope; the allocator and the radix layer enforce the isolation.

Appendix P RoPE pairing convention: the post-hoc fix on MLA

The kernel referenced in Section 3.3 initially hardcoded the NEOX (half-split) pairing of RoPE dims (pairing index ii with i+d/2i{+}d/2 via 𝚛𝚘𝚝𝚊𝚝𝚎​_​𝚑𝚊𝚕𝚏\mathtt{rotate\_half}). MLA on DeepSeek-V2-Lite uses interleaved (GPT-J) pairing (mixing 2​i,2​i+12i,2i{+}1). The mismatch leaves Kpe⋅cosK_{\mathrm{pe}}\cdot\cos correct but corrupts the sin⁡(Δ​f)\sin(\Delta f)-rotated half, hiding at Δ→0\Delta{\to}0 and growing with |Δ||\Delta|. The fix is a small helper that reads rotary_emb.is_neox_style and applies the matching pairing; the path for half-split models (Llama, Qwen2) is arithmetically identical to the prior code. Post-fix bit-exact validation against a single-rotation reference covers Δ∈{1,21,48,76,512,2000}\Delta\in\{1,21,48,76,512,2000\} on a hand-built (model-independent) cos/sin cache; the end-to-end bit-exact check on the live serving stack covers |Δ||\Delta| up to ≈4531\approx 4531, with target positions past original_max_position_embeddings=4096{=}4096 to exercise the YaRN-interpolated regime. Full provenance and the bit-exact unit test live in scratch/rope_convention_fix_test.py.

Appendix Q bf16 K-storage precision floor

Distinct from the rotation primitive’s mathematical correctness, the bf16 KV pool imposes a structural per-K-entry precision floor. We sweep the rotation kernel at fixed sources {10,100,1000,4000,8000,8836}\{10,100,1000,4000,8000,8836\} and signed deltas up to |Δ|=6794|\Delta|{=}6794, comparing against an fp32 reference and a bf16-throughout path:

  • •

    fp32 (entire path in single precision): max-abs error per K entry of 1.4×10−61.4{\times}10^{-6} at (p=10,Δ=1)(p{=}10,\Delta{=}1), growing to ∼1.6×10−3{\sim}1.6{\times}10^{-3} at (p=8836,Δ=6794)(p{=}8836,\Delta{=}6794) — the kernel’s mathematical precision floor under finite-position fp32 cos/sin.

  • •

    bf16 (cos/sin and KV pool both bf16): error saturates at ∼\sim1–3% per entry at every (p,Δ)(p,\Delta) tested, including (p=10,Δ=1)(p{=}10,\Delta{=}1).

The bf16 floor is independent of Δ\Delta; it is the inherent quantization noise of storing KK in bf16 in the pool. Argmax flips happen on prompts whose top-1 vs top-2 logit gap is smaller than the noise; on the 50-step long-context replay of Section 5, 48/5048/50 first-token outputs are bit-identical to the full-prefill reference, the remaining two differing in cases where the model’s logit margin lies below the floor. The mitigation (AKASHA_PIC_ROTATION_FP32, on by default) runs cos/sin in fp32 and downcasts the rotated KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} to bf16 on the way to the pool, matching the model’s own attention-forward dtype policy; this removes the rotation computation’s contribution to the floor but does not eliminate the bf16 storage contribution. The data is in scratch/rope_bf16_precision_probe.py; the engineering note is in docs/feedback/BF16_ROTATION_PRECISION_FLOOR_2026-05-28.md.

Appendix R Role B: radix-trie pre-population via insert + re-match

Two integration paths share the rotation kernel. Role A (the original) intercepts match_prefix, returns a patched MatchResult with borrowed slots appended, and tracks the borrowed slots on the request for free at cache_finished_req. Role B Level 2 goes one layer further: after a successful splice, it calls tree_cache.insert(InsertParams(key=token_ids[:cur_prefix_end], value=concat(orig_indices, dst_slots))) and re-runs the un-wrapped match_prefix (stashed at install time as tree_cache._akasha_orig_match_prefix) to obtain a native, longer trie match. The scheduler’s inc_lock_ref then locks the new last node, the slots are owned by the radix trie, and the borrowed-slot orphan-detection retires. Future requests with the same prefix match the spliced range natively via match_prefix, without any Leyline hook at lookup time. Correctness check: on the cross-tenant validation answered_correctly_frac is identical between Role B L2 on and off across both tenants at C=1C{=}1 and C=4C{=}4. The architectural design and the lock-ref ordering argument are in docs/feedback/ROLE_B_RADIX_PREPOPULATOR_2026-05-27.md.

Appendix S Manifest warm-start for cross-tenant discovery

At C>1C{>}1, peer requests in the same batch all call match_prefix before any has finished prefill; the popular registry entries are not yet visible, and the splice attempts walk chunks at positions that miss the registry. We close this race by serializing {content​_​hash,chunk​_​tokens,count,first​_​observed}\{\mathrm{content\_hash},\mathrm{chunk\_tokens},\mathrm{count},\mathrm{first\_observed}\} tuples to a JSONL manifest at runtime (incrementally on first observation of each new unique hash, so the file is correct under abrupt termination), and at startup replaying each chunk’s tokens as a /generate request to the live server before the benchmark begins. SGLang’s cache_finished_req hook then populates both the PIC registry and the radix trie with valid slot indices for every manifest chunk.

Empirically (Cross-tenant cell of Section 5, C=4C{=}4, 22 tenants ×\times 3232 requests, 88 articles, 15001500-character bodies): without warm-start, cand_total=6{=}6, chunks_spliced=2{=}2; with warm-start of the same workload’s prior-run manifest (1515 unique chunks, ∼\sim4 KB), cand_total=96{=}96, chunks_spliced=16{=}16, tenant-1 p50p_{50} e2e drops from 1.0161.016 s to 0.9530.953 s (−6.2%-6.2\%). The warm-up phase completes in ∼1.2{\sim}1.2 s. The mechanism is gated by AKASHA_PIC_MANIFEST_OUT on the producer and AKASHA_PIC_MANIFEST_IN on the consumer; replay code is at tools/akasha_warmup_replay.py. The cold-start gap (the very first run with no manifest) is unfixed by this mechanism and is named in Numerics.; the design discussion is in docs/feedback/CONC4_DISCOVERY_GAP_DESIGN_2026-05-28.md.

Appendix T Real-trace long-context replay

The synthetic three-arm microbenchmark of Appendix B establishes that the splice mechanism is alive in a production SGLang scheduler at fixed-template prompts. We additionally measure on a real agentic trajectory (07be28b9/shopping_cart from a debug-gym capture (Yuan et al., 2025)): 50 steps, prompts growing from 334 to ≈28\approx 28K tokens, C=1C{=}1. Vanilla RadixCache reaches sum-e2e 52.6552.65 s (27.6%27.6\% replay cache-hit). Leyline (Role B L2 + fp32 rotation) reaches 49.8549.85 s (27.8%27.8\% replay cache-hit), a 5.3%5.3\% wall-clock improvement; cross-arm first-token agreement against the radix arm is 48/5048/50 (the remaining two land on prompts inside the bf16 floor of Appendix Q). Decomposing by ablating one toggle at a time: fp32 rotation on / Role B L2 off reaches 49.6249.62 s — within run-to-run variance of the full configuration. Role B L2 is timing-neutral at this single-trajectory scale (the architectural benefit, cross-request amortization through a populated trie, requires more same-prefix repeats than 50 steps provides); fp32 rotation contributes essentially all of the e2e win. A second trajectory (0f724375/shopping_cart, 91.6%91.6\% RadixCache hit rate, fewer divergent tail tokens per step) returns splice 0.6%0.6\% slower than radix and 20/2020/20 bit-identical — consistent with the prediction that splice has nothing to do when RadixCache already covers the workload.

Appendix U KV bytes attributable to splice

Per-token KV in the DSv2-Lite MLA pool is (kv​_​lora​_​rank+qk​_​rope​_​head​_​dim)×nlayers×bytes​_​per​_​dtype=(512+64)×27×2=31,104(\mathrm{kv\_lora\_rank}+\mathrm{qk\_rope\_head\_dim})\times n_{\mathrm{layers}}\times\mathrm{bytes\_per\_dtype}=(512+64)\times 27\times 2=31{,}104 bytes (≈30.4{\approx}30.4 KB). Per-run KV-bytes attributable to splice across the configurations of this paper:

  • •

    Cross-tenant C=1C{=}1, no warm-start: 55 chunks ×51\times 51 tokens =256=256 tokens, 7.967.96 MB.

  • •

    Cross-tenant C=4C{=}4, no warm-start: 22 chunks ×64\times 64 tokens, 3.983.98 MB.

  • •

    Cross-tenant C=4C{=}4, with warm-start (Appendix S): 1616 chunks ×56\times 56 tokens average, 27.8727.87 MB (7×7{\times} no-warmup).

  • •

    Long-context agentic replay (Appendix T): +1,750+1{,}750 tokens cached over the radix arm, ≈52.5\approx 52.5 MB.

These are the splice’s incremental contribution to cached KV content over vanilla RadixCache; the splice still allocates fresh dst slots per request, so peak occupancy of the KV pool is not directly reduced — only re-computation is. The data is in scratch/kv_savings_audit.py.

Peak pool occupancy (2×22{\times}2 matrix).

We instrumented the SGLang TokenToKVPoolAllocator via PICCache.sample_pool_occupancy(tree_cache, source) called inside the writeback wrap of cache_finished_req and cache_unfinished_req. Each call records (ts, avail, total, source) as one line of a per-process JSONL stream (AKASHA_PIC_POOL_OCCUPANCY_OUT); writes are incremental rather than at atexit so SLURM/SIGTERM teardown cannot lose data. The total pool size on our DSv2-Lite configuration is 1,698,8461{,}698{,}846 slots (the same number across runs since model and engine flags are fixed); peak occupancy is computed as total−mint⁡(availt)\mathrm{total}-\min_{t}(\mathrm{avail}_{t}). We ran four arms on the cross-tenant Zipf workload (C=4C{=}4, 15001500-character article bodies, 3232 requests/tenant):

  • •

    A: 2-tenant, splice ON + manifest warm-start. 147147 samples, peak 2,1112{,}111 slots (65.765.7 MB); 1616 chunks spliced (cand_total 9696).

  • •

    B: 2-tenant, splice OFF. 133133 samples, peak 1,7241{,}724 slots (53.653.6 MB).

  • •

    C: 4-tenant, splice ON, no warm-start. 135135 samples, peak 3,1353{,}135 slots (97.597.5 MB); 44 chunks spliced (cand_total 66, hit by the conc=4 discovery gap).

  • •

    D: 4-tenant, splice OFF. 135135 samples, peak 3,1353{,}135 slots (97.597.5 MB).

Same-tenant-count ON-vs-OFF deltas are +12.0+12.0 MB at 2 tenants (warm-up-preloaded articles staying trie-pinned, plus 1414 extra warmup requests growing the trie) and 0.00.0 MB at 4 tenants (spliced chunks inserted by reference, no fresh slots freed, same slot count as OFF). We later extended the tenant sweep to 3 and 8 tenants with splice-OFF and splice-ON (no-warmup) at C=4C{=}4, plus 2-tenant warm-start at C=8C{=}8, on the same Zipf workload (jobs 473946473946–473952473952). The splice-OFF curve is monotone sub-linear and grows the savings with tenant count:

  • •

    2 tenants →\to 3 tenants: 53.6→74.353.6\to 74.3 MB (1.39×1.39\times vs linear 1.5×1.5\times; 7.67.6 pp savings).

  • •

    2 tenants →\to 4 tenants: 53.6→97.553.6\to 97.5 MB (1.82×1.82\times vs linear 2.0×2.0\times; 9.09.0 pp).

  • •

    2 tenants →\to 8 tenants: 53.6→182.053.6\to 182.0 MB (3.40×3.40\times vs linear 4.0×4.0\times; 15.015.0 pp).

Splice ON (without warm-start) is indistinguishable from OFF at every tenant count we measured beyond 2: 3-tenant 74.374.3 MB vs 74.374.3 MB, 4-tenant 97.597.5 MB vs 97.597.5 MB, 8-tenant 182.0182.0 MB vs 182.0182.0 MB. The mechanism does not change peak pool occupancy — inserts into the radix trie are by reference, and the warmup-preloaded chunks (when present) raise peak by 1212–1515 MB regardless of whether the live workload reaches splice activation.

The discovery side of these arms is the bottleneck. We observed cand_total=0{=}0 in every splice-ON arm except the original 2-tenant C=4C{=}4 + warmup (arm A), including 3-tenant no-warmup (1515 splice-loop entries, all empty), 4-tenant no-warmup with reduced Narticles=4N_{\textrm{articles}}{=}4, 8-tenant no-warmup (4040 entries), and 2-tenant C=8C{=}8 warm-up (2222 entries). The registry was populated in every case (1515–3535 unique hashes observed) and the splice loop entered as expected; the candidate filter (src_kv_indices is not None and request_id ≠\neq rid_now) returned the empty set, consistent with the warmup-time slots having been freed by the time the workload’s first batch reaches match_prefix. The fix is concrete (run warmup-replay in a separate process pre-startup, or extend the registry to retain a fetchable representation past the warmup request’s lifetime) and is parked as follow-up work distinct from the directive contract. The JSONL streams live at results/pool_occupancy/{A,B,C,D,E,E2,F,G,H,I,J,K,L}_*.jsonl; analyzers are scratch/pool_occupancy_audit.py and scratch/kv_117_full_audit.py.

Edit-shape headroom (arm F, 473946473946).

To quantify what a multi-segment splice (Appendix V discussion of cross-instance reuse; design sketch in docs/feedback/MULTI_SEGMENT_EDIT_SHAPE_DESIGN_2026-05-28.md) would unlock, we ran a 2-tenant C=4C{=}4 + warmup arm with the new AKASHA_XTENANT_EDIT_WINDOW_CHARS=128 knob (added to cross_tenant.py; replaces a 128128-character window at the middle of each article body with per-occurrence-deterministic random text, holding the position fixed so chunks before and after the edit align across occurrences via CDC’s content-defined boundaries). The result: the registry observed 8989 unique hashes (6×6\times baseline arm A’s 1515), peak pool occupancy reached 371.5371.5 MB (5.7×5.7\times baseline A’s 65.765.7 MB), and 39/15939/159 chunks hit the observe path — evidence the edit-shape does materialize the [shared prefix] [unique edit] [shared suffix] structure expected. The current splice loop’s break-on-first-miss caps phase-1 discovery (and the candidate-filter issue above further empties cand_total at the splice loop’s entry); a phase-2 continuation hook firing from cache_unfinished_req after the engine prefills the edit window would, by construction, recover the suffix chunks — worth on the order of 371−65≈300371-65\approx 300 MB of edit-related pinned KV in this synthetic configuration. The phase-2 implementation is gated on production workloads with naturally-occurring edit-shape (code-completion agents that revise earlier turns, user-driven chat correction flows); the workload-side scaffolding is in place.

Follow-up arm E: 4-tenant warm-start.

A fifth arm exercises the manifest warm-start at C=4C{=}4 (147147 samples, peak 3,6133{,}613 slots = 112.4112.4 MB, +15+15 MB above arm D’s 97.597.5 MB from the same warmup-pinned-articles mechanism as arm A’s +12+12 MB at C=2C{=}2). The pool-occupancy delta is consistent with the arm-A/B pattern. The splice-discovery side of E, however, exhibited an unexpected cand_total=0{=}0 despite a fully populated registry (3535 unique hashes observed, of which only 22 broke on first-chunk hash-miss across 3535 splice-loop entries; reproduced with AKASHA_PIC_ROLE_B_L2∈{0,1}{\in}\{0,1\} as arm E2, jobs 472782472782/472792472792). The candidate-filter degenerate at C=4C{=}4 when both warmup and live workload populate the same registry concurrently is a known limitation isolated by this measurement; the occupancy claim above does not depend on it, and the splice’s chunk-discovery throughput at C=4C{=}4 is therefore reported from the no-warmup arm C, not from E. Investigating this filter interaction is parked as a follow-up — the proximate path-of-least-effort is to run warmup-replay in a separate process pre-startup (rather than against the live server), so the warmup-time and workload-time observations don’t share a registry mutator window. The pool-occupancy stream for E is at results/pool_occupancy/E_4tenant_spliceon_warmup.jsonl.

Appendix V Related-work positioning: position-shifted vs cross-instance reuse

The Leyline contribution lives at the position-shifted reuse layer: a kernel that rotates cached KpeK_{\mathrm{pe}} by Δ\Delta so a single instance can reuse content at shifted positions, plus the directive abstraction that lets a policy drive that rotation. The cross-session sharing verb (Appendix J) and the warm-start manifest (Appendix S) are the first steps of a complementary layer: cross-process / cross-instance content reuse. The two share content-hash addressing as their handle on identity. The cross-instance KV transfer story (live byte movement between GPU pools across a cluster, with the consumer applying the Leyline-style rotation on top of the transferred bytes) is the natural extension; we treat the manifest as the static-disk version of what a live RDMA fetch would do dynamically. The infrastructure for that live fetch is the subject of follow-up work and is out of scope here.

Appendix W Responsible research checklist

This appendix concentrates the items of the ACL Rolling Review Responsible Research Checklist that warrant separate elaboration. Item A1 (Limitations) is satisfied by the dedicated Limitations section preceding the bibliography.

A2 Potential risks.

Leyline is a serving-side mechanism for KV-cache editing; it does not alter the model weights, training data, or output content. Two deploy-side risks warrant explicit naming, both already surfaced in Limitations and the [RFC] Pinned Caching thread (vLLM Project contributors, 2024): (i) cross-tenant prefix-cache leakage under content-addressed caching admits a prefix-guessing side-channel, which explicit user-keyed partitioning at deploy time closes; (ii) user-issued retention directives in future deployments could exhaust KV memory, requiring per-request fail-fast policy. Neither is a property of the directive abstraction itself; both are deploy-side policy work.

B Scientific artifacts (overview).

We use four open-weight MLA models, the SGLang serving stack, and the debug-gym mini_nightmare benchmark. We create a ∼200{\sim}200-LOC patch to SGLang’s RadixCache plus a Python LeylineCacheManager class.

B1 Citations of creators.

All artifacts are cited at first mention in the main text: DeepSeek-V2-Lite (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2024a), JoyAI-LLM Flash (Cai et al., 2026), GLM-4.7-Flash (Team GLM and others, 2024), Moonlight-16B-A3B (Moonshot AI, 2025), SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024), debug-gym (Yuan et al., 2025).

B2 Licenses.

All artifacts we use are released under permissive open-source licenses suitable for academic research: the four MLA models under their respective Hugging Face model-card licenses (MIT or Apache-2.0 equivalents); SGLang under Apache-2.0; debug-gym under the upstream Microsoft research license. Our Leyline patch is released under Apache-2.0, consistent with the upstream SGLang project.

B3 Intended use.

Each used artifact was released for research and benchmarking; our use is consistent. The MLA models are intended for inference research; debug-gym is intended as an agentic-debugging benchmark; SGLang is intended as a research-and-production serving stack. Our patch is intended for research use on top of SGLang and inherits its access terms.

B4 PII / offensive content.

debug-gym mini_nightmare consists of three synthetic Python debugging tasks (counter, shopping_cart, sum_tree); the inputs are program source and hidden tests, containing no human-generated natural-language text, no personally identifying information, and no offensive content. Our experiments do not involve human-subject data collection.

B5 Documentation of artifacts.

Documentation of used artifacts is at their respective project pages (Hugging Face model cards, debug-gym repository, SGLang documentation). The Leyline patch is documented via its inline code release accompanying the camera-ready.

B6 Data statistics.

The deployment evaluation (Section 5) covers 8 debug-gym mini_nightmare tasks ×\times 4 seeds ×\times 2 policy conditions (truncate_older_than:n=2 as treatment, keep_all as baseline), with 32 baseline + 33 treatment reliable trials and a 50-step trajectory cap per cell, run under the post-2026-05-26 harness fix described in B2. A ninth mini_nightmare task, pandas_dataframe, was excluded because it requires fetching the Titanic CSV over the network and our compute nodes have no outbound internet access; both policies failed equally on every pandas_dataframe trial we ran (max-steps reached with zero score on 0/3 completed; 5/8 trials terminated in the download retry loop). All returned trials carry policy_loaded=1 in their per-trial metadata. The stub ablation (Appendix M) covers 4 stub modes ×\times 3 trajectories ×\times 2 models. The multi-step replay (Appendix D) is a single 12-step counter trajectory replayed under three execution paths.

C1 Model size and compute budget.

Parameter counts: DeepSeek-V2-Lite (16B total / 2.4B active), JoyAI-LLM Flash (48B total / 3B active), GLM-4.7-Flash (30B / 3B), Moonlight-16B-A3B (16B / 3B). All experiments are inference-only; no model training. Experiments ran on an internal HPC cluster (institution withheld for anonymity) under mixed GPU configurations: GLM-4.7-Flash and JoyAI-LLM Flash served on 4×4{\times} NVIDIA H200 with SGLang tensor-parallelism (TP==4); Moonlight-16B-A3B on 2×2{\times} H100; DeepSeek-V2-Lite on 1×1{\times} H100; auxiliary single-GPU probes (stub ablation, short-trajectory replays) on 1×1{\times} H200 or 1×1{\times} H100. Per-trajectory wall-clock is on the order of minutes, and the full sweep fits in single-digit GPU-days. Leyline’s own kernel overhead is microsecond-scale per slot per the bound inherited from Ma et al. (2026); we do not report end-to-end latency at production batch sizes here (see Limitations).

C2 Experimental setup and hyperparameters.

Sampling parameters follow each model’s recommended defaults. Policy hyperparameters in Section 5: truncate_older_than(n=2, max_chars=200, tools=bash) as treatment, keep_all as baseline. Trajectory cap: 50 steps. Seeds: 4 per cell. We did not run a hyperparameter search; the chosen n=2n{=}2 threshold is the single point on the policy-aggressiveness axis at which the treatment-vs-baseline contrast is reported.

C3 Descriptive statistics.

Solve-rate numbers in Section 5 are aggregated across 4 seeds per (task, policy) cell; Table 2 reports per-task fractions and the overall sum. The paired (task, seed)-cell-level disagreement analysis quoted in Section 5 (99 treatment-wins vs 55 baseline-wins) restricts to the 14 of 31 paired cells where the two policies disagreed on the binary solve outcome. Tool-name agreement in Table 4 is measured per-step over a 12-step counter trajectory under Leyline versus the full-context baseline.

C4 Package versions.

SGLang 0.5.2 with the Leyline patch; debug-gym 1.3.0.

D Human subjects.

The work does not involve human annotators, human participants, or human-subject data of any kind. Items D1–D4 are therefore not applicable.
